source_units.heading: Explanation steps
source_units.text:
## Explanation steps

Origin: reused complete checked passage [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/Climate_Scenarios_Policy_and_Adaptation.md#Climate scenarios, policy and adaptation]]; fingerprint `dc3f2be26999e63b812767c1b200564516dc4fb9a19243829ec7abf3f0ff1c90`. Heading depth alone is adapted.

### Climate scenarios, policy and adaptation

A climate scenario asks what follows **if** a coherent set of social, technological, emissions and policy conditions occurs. It is not an assigned probability or an unconditional forecast. The lecture uses older RCP projections alongside newer SSP-labelled examples; the two naming systems and their temperature baselines must be distinguished. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=40|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 40–45]]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 A[Socioeconomic assumptions] --> B[Emissions pathway]
 C[Policy choices] --> B
 B --> D[Concentrations and radiative forcing]
 D --> E[Conditional climate projection]
 E --> F[Impacts and risks]
 C --> G[Mitigation reduces drivers]
 F --> H[Adaptation manages remaining impacts]
 I[Scenario label period baseline uncertainty] --> E
```

This map follows pp. 40–45 and 43's paired emissions/concentration graphic; it explains why the policy discussion needs both mitigation and adaptation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=40|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 40–45]]

#### SSP assumptions and RCP forcing pathways

The source presents **SSP2**, “middle of the road,” as its baseline socioeconomic narrative, extending major development trends without a large assumed policy/technology break. That is the lecture's baseline choice, not a universal definition that SSP2 equals one forcing outcome. Shared Socioeconomic Pathways describe demographic, economic and technological narratives; Representative Concentration Pathways describe emissions/concentration/forcing trajectories. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=41|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 41, 43]]

Radiative forcing measures a change in Earth's energy balance in **W/m²**, as the embedded comments on pp. 41–42 explain. RCP labels 2.6/4.5/6.0/8.5 refer to approximate 2100 forcing levels, with different trajectories toward them. The source associates 2.6/4.5/6.0 with approximately 490/650/850 ppm CO2-equivalent and leaves 8.5 unfinished. These are the slide's older shorthand values, not concentrations of CO2 alone; the exact trajectory and whether a quoted value is a peak or endpoint matter. Its claim that forcing is “declining” should not be read as monotonic decline throughout every RCP. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=41|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 41]]

There is a source inconsistency: p. 41 calls RCP6.0 “close to SSP2,” whereas p. 42 calls RCP8.5 “close to SSP2.” A socioeconomic family does not uniquely identify a forcing path. **Authoritative clarification:** IPCC AR6 WGI SPM BoxSPM.1 and note 22 define **SSPx-y** as socioeconomic family x plus approximate 2100 forcing y. The supplied p. 43 itself shows SSP2-4.5 as intermediate, alongside SSP1-1.9/SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0/SSP5-8.5. [IPCC AR6 WGI SPM, BoxSPM.1/note22](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/summary-for-policymakers/). Thus neither conflicting “close to” statement is used as a one-to-one mapping. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=41|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 41–43]]

#### The AR5 temperature table needs its reference period

The supplied p. 42 table reports the following **°C changes relative to 1986–2005**, verified from IPCC 2014 Synthesis Report Table 2.1 (printed p. 60 and its notes). That missing baseline is essential: these are not automatically additional temperatures above the Paris preindustrial reference. Entries are means with the source's likely ranges; scenarios are conditional, and range width is not a probability assigned to the scenario itself. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=42|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 42]]

| RCP |2046–2065 mean (likely range),°C|2081–2100 mean (likely range),°C|
|---|---|---|
|2.6|1.0 (0.4–1.6)|1.0 (0.3–1.7)|
|4.5|1.4 (0.9–2.0)|1.8 (1.1–2.6)|
|6.0|1.3 (0.8–1.8)|2.2 (1.4–3.1)|
|8.5|2.0 (1.4–2.6)|3.7 (2.6–4.8)|

The official table notes natural variability, forcing/model uncertainty and different confidence for the two horizons. Its observed baseline offset is not itself a complete uncertainty conversion rule, so do not add a constant and reuse the identical uncertainty range without qualification. [IPCC2014 Synthesis Report, Table2.1 and notes](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full.pdf). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=42|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 42]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Emissions_Concentration_Scenarios.png]]

Physical p. 43 compares annual CO2 emissions (billions of tonnes/year) with resulting atmospheric CO2 concentrations (ppm). Low-emission paths bend down and can become net negative; concentrations need not follow emissions one-for-one because they reflect accumulated additions and removals. The caption says only central illustrative curves are shown, not the full uncertainty distribution. This graphic therefore illustrates scenario mechanisms rather than exact forecasts. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=43|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 43]]

#### Climate policy: source claims and verified chronology

Physical p. 44 names the UNFCCC, Kyoto arrangements and annual Conferences of the Parties (COPs). It refers to Annex I/II groupings and writes “DCM, JI”; the recognized Kyoto project mechanism is **CDM, Clean Development Mechanism**, alongside Joint Implementation. Annex groupings/targets are not all interchangeable: the official Kyoto overview distinguishes the Convention's annex structure and Kyoto Annex B commitments. Only that overview is needed here, not an invented treaty-law curriculum. **Correction:** the slide's “1996 Kyoto Protocol” is wrong; Kyoto was adopted 11 December 1997 and entered into force 16 February 2005. [UNFCCC Kyoto overview, opening/market mechanisms](https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-kyoto-protocol). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=44|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 44]]

The lecture describes Paris COP21 in 2015 as pursuing warming well below 2°C and efforts toward 1.5°C above preindustrial levels, with peaking as soon as possible and rapid subsequent reductions. Its discussion of INDCs concerns the pledges at that historical conference, not a checked present-day assessment of every NDC. The slide calls 4 November 2016 a “ratification” date; it is the Agreement's **entry into force** date. Adoption was 12 December 2015; individual parties ratify on their own dates. [UNFCCC Paris overview](https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-paris-agreement). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=44|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 44]]

The slide's subsequent conference list runs through COP30/Brazil 2025, naming Marrakesh 2016, Bonn 2017, Katowice 2018, Madrid 2019, the 2020 pandemic gap, Glasgow 2021, Cairo 2022, Dubai 2023 and Baku 2024. **Location correction:** COP27 was in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, not Cairo; the official proceedings state its 2022 venue. [UNFCCC COP27 proceedings listing](https://unfccc.int/event/cop-27). These are the source's historical orientation, not a live future meeting schedule. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=44|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 44]]

#### Mitigation and adaptation solve different parts of the problem

Mitigation reduces climate-change drivers, such as net greenhouse-gas emissions; adaptation changes exposure/vulnerability and responses to climatic effects that still occur. Physical p. 45 combines a historical/projected warming panel with five escalating risk categories—unique/threatened systems, extreme weather, distribution of impacts, global aggregate impacts and large-scale singular events. Coloured transitions represent increasing risk, not cash damages or a uniform threshold for all outcomes. It overlays Paris NDC/aspiration labels on an AR5-era figure and concludes that even successful mitigation leaves impacts requiring adaptation. Read the overlay as a teaching illustration, not a current quantified forecast of the Paris pledges. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=45|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 45]]

The core reading path is assumptions→emissions→forcing→conditional climate→risks, then the complementary responses. Matching scenario type, baseline, date and uncertainty is prerequisite to using the numbers; conference chronology is supporting context with the source errors explicitly repaired here. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=40|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 40–45]]

source_units.heading: Worked example
source_units.text:
## Worked example

O019-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. **Prompt:** Using the source AR5table, scenario RCP2.6 has mean warming 1.0°C for 2046–2065 and 1.0°C for 2081–2100; scenario RCP8.5 has late mean 3.7°C. State the reference period, compute within-scenario mean change and late between-scenario difference, and explain why these are not automatically Paris preindustrial warming or probabilities. Explain SSP2 versus RCP and SSP2-4.5, source conflicting SSP2 mappings and forcing versus concentration units. Classify “reduce fossil-fuel greenhouse emissions” and “protect exposed communities from remaining floods” as mitigation/adaptation and explain remaining risk. Correct the supplied historical claims “Kyoto 1996,” “4 November 2016 Paris ratification” and “COP27 Cairo”; distinguish verified chronology from an invented current policy or conference schedule.

**Complete solution and essential rubric:** AR5changes are relative to 1986–2005. For scenario RCP2.6, the difference of displayed means is$1.0-1.0=0.000000^\circ\mathrm{C}$; late between-scenario mean gap is$3.7-1.0=2.700000^\circ\mathrm{C}$. These mean differences are not new uncertainty intervals: preserve each likely range and model/natural-variability/horizon qualifications. They are conditional projections, not assigned scenario probabilities or automatically values above preindustrial conditions. SSPs describe socioeconomic narratives; RCPs describe forcing pathways. SSP2 alone does not uniquely select a forcing path, and SSP2-4.5 combines socioeconomic family 2 with approximate 2100 forcing 4.5 W/m². The source’s RCP6.0/8.5 “close to SSP2” statements conflict and are not used as unique mappings. Older ppm CO2e shorthand is forcing-equivalent concentration, not CO2 alone or GWP-weighted tonnes. The first action reduces climate drivers (mitigation); the second manages remaining exposure/vulnerability (adaptation). Even successful mitigation leaves some impacts; the source’s coloured risk categories are neither cash damages nor one uniform threshold. Kyoto was adopted 11 December 1997 and entered into force 16 February 2005; the mechanism is CDM with JI, not DCM. Paris adoption 12 December 2015 and entry 4 November 2016 are distinct from each party’s ratification date. COP27 was Sharm el-Sheikh, not Cairo. These bounded historical corrections and source COP30/Brazil 2025 pointer are not a checked live timetable or present NDC-effect assessment. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

source_units.text:
## Rubric and independence

Required components: scenario_type_forcing_and_concentration, baseline_mean_comparison_and_uncertainty, mitigation_adaptation_and_historical_policy_limits. Each full prompt/key below elicits every component; all are necessary for a pass on every permitted pair. Accept algebraically equivalent expressions and clearly defined opposite cash-flow signs with correct interpretation. A pass requires all requested outputs/reasons, correct units/assumptions and no critical conceptual error. Partial means a missing component or an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip with an otherwise valid method; independent correction is required for a pass. Fail means a critical mechanism/condition is wrong. Unscorable means a response or its help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown help conditions are never independent evidence.

Critical errors: SSP2 forced into unique RCP; scenario range interpreted as scenario probability; AR5 baseline silently called preindustrial; adaptation treated as replacing all mitigation; historical source meeting list treated as current schedule.

Acquisition requires two distinct unused unassisted full checks selected from the six exact metadata routes. Every I/D form covers all components; W1, S1, the prerequisite and C1 are forbidden substitutes. A D form used for acquisition cannot later be counted again as delayed success. No teach-generated item may replace a named full check; additional verified explanation/practice is allowed under the unchanged method and may not fabricate evidence. If fewer than two fresh forms remain for acquisition, return a plan_issue for an additional prepared bank.

| Component | I1 | I2 | D1 | D2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|

An observed omitted term/sign is tentative until the learner explains it; compare the reasoning with the critical errors above. Score the original response before providing help. Route a conceptual failure to the relevant included derivation and prerequisite, then use an unused full form.

O019-C1, item_version 1, narrow_correction. **Prompt:** Does SSP2 alone define RCP8.5, and does an AR5warming range relative to 1986–2005automatically equal warming above preindustrial? **Key/rubric:** No to both. Socioeconomic family and forcing trajectory are separate labels; temperature reference periods must be matched with a justified comparison. The source conflicts do not supply a unique mapping. source_units.heading: Four environmental functions
source_units.text:
## Four environmental functions

The slides distinguish four ways in which the environment matters to the economy. These functions can coexist in the same place. The forest example shows the distinction particularly clearly: wood is a resource, while aesthetic, cultural and recreational enjoyment belongs to the separate category of demand services. This comparison is an explanatory synthesis of the examples on slide 2. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 2]]

### Resources

Resources provide inputs or possibilities for economic activity. Slide 2 distinguishes **non-degradable resources**, with sunshine, wind and waves as examples, from **degradable resources**. Within the latter group it distinguishes renewable resources, such as wood and biomass, from non-renewable or exhaustible resources, such as fossil fuels and minerals. It also lists space as a resource. Keep this source taxonomy when interpreting the later diagram: the slide uses “renewable” for the wood/biomass category and separately lists sunshine, wind and waves as non-degradable. It does not supply a broader taxonomy or a formal definition of “degradable.” [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 2]]

The distinction becomes economically meaningful when resource use is compared with replenishment. An exhaustible resource can be reduced by extraction. For renewable resources, the diagram separately represents harvesting above and below yield or growth, so “renewable” alone does not establish that a particular pattern of use maintains the resource. The relevant question is how fast the resource is used relative to how fast it grows. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 2 and 4]]

### Sinks and assimilative capacity

A **sink** is a place where undesirable outputs, including emissions and wastes, may be placed. The source describes this function through **assimilative capacity**: the environment's capacity to receive or assimilate those outputs. The diagram later compares waste with that capacity. This makes waste disposal part of the environment–economy relationship, alongside resource extraction. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 2 and 4]]

The capacity comparison matters because the diagram assigns different consequences to waste below capacity and waste above capacity. The existence of a sink therefore does not establish that every amount of waste has the same consequences. The source supplies a qualitative threshold comparison; it does not quantify a safe emissions level, a pollutant-specific assimilation rate, or the time needed for assimilation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4]]

### Demand services

The environment also supplies services people value directly. Slide 2 names aesthetic, cultural and recreational services, such as those provided by a forest. In the full diagram, the environmental resource node has a positive amenity connection to utility. Thus the environment contributes to wellbeing through more than goods produced by firms and consumed by households. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 2 and 4]]

**Utility**, denoted by $U$, is the diagram's representation of wellbeing or benefit. The source identifies utility flows but gives no numerical utility scale, utility function, or valuation method. The positive amenity arrow establishes a direction of effect in this schematic framework; it does not report a measured monetary benefit. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4]]

### Global biospheric life-supporting services

The fourth category concerns the systems that support life more generally. The source names the climate system, hydrologic cycle and soil production. These services place the production-and-consumption relationship in a wider biospheric setting. They explain why environmental economics considers systemic conditions as well as individual resource inputs and enjoyable amenities. This final sentence is a synthesis of the category's role in the introductory framework. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 2]]

source_units.text:
## The economic core: firms and households

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Intro_Slide_03_Economic_Core.png]]

*Economic core reproduced from 00_Intro.pptx, slide 3, through a local LibreOffice PDF rendering. Firms represent production ($P$), households represent consumption ($C$), and the figure also labels $K$, labour, savings, wages, and rent/interest.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 3]]

Read the figure first as an economic relationship. Firms produce what households consume. Labour and savings appear above the two groups, while wages and rent/interest appear below them. The loop beside firms is labelled $K$, the conventional capital symbol; the source gives no separate definition or numerical relationship for $K$. The point of the next slide is to place this compact economic core inside the wider resource, waste and utility network. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 3–4]]

source_units.heading: Reading the physical and utility network
source_units.text:
## Reading the physical and utility network

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Intro_Slide_04_Environment_Economy_Network.png]]

*Environment–economy network reproduced from 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4. Solid arrows denote flows of materials/energy; dashed arrows denote utility flows. The blue highlight locates production and consumption within the wider network. Plus and minus signs show qualitative directions of effect.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4]]

The symbols supplied by the slide are:

| Symbol | Source meaning |
|---|---|
| $P$ | Production |
| $C$ | Consumption |
| $U$ | Utility |
| $R$ | Natural resources |
| $ER$ | Exhaustible resources |
| $RR$ | Renewable resources |
| $h$ | Harvest rate |
| $y$ | Yield/growth |
| $W$ | Waste |
| $A$ | Assimilative capacity |

The diagram also contains a lower-case $r$ on the return path from waste toward resources. The source's printed legend does not define $r$. The path can be identified visually as a material return path, but this note does not assign it a verified name, rate, or equation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4, lower-left return path and legend]]

### Resource use and replenishment

The main horizontal physical path runs from natural resources ($R$) through production ($P$) to consumption ($C$). The resource branch separates exhaustible resources ($ER$) and renewable resources ($RR$). On the exhaustible branch, the displayed case $h>y$ connects with a negative sign. On the renewable branch, $h>y$ has a negative sign, whereas $h<y$ has a positive sign. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4, left resource branches]]

These inequalities compare harvesting with yield or growth. If harvesting exceeds growth, use runs ahead of replenishment and the diagram represents a reduction of the resource. If harvesting is below growth on the renewable branch, replenishment can exceed removal and the diagram represents a positive effect on that resource. For this interpretation, $h$ and $y$ must refer to comparable quantities over the same time interval. This comparability is a mathematical requirement of reading the inequality, rather than a separate numerical assumption supplied by the slide. The diagram does not specify a growth function, units, a time horizon, or an equality case $h=y$. It therefore supports directional reasoning, rather than a calculation of a sustainable harvest level. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4]]

### Waste and capacity

Solid paths from the resource, production and consumption parts of the diagram join the waste node $W$. Waste then connects to assimilative capacity $A$. Two cases appear below it: $W<A$ and $W>A$. The $W<A$ branch returns to resources with a positive sign. The $W>A$ branch returns with a negative sign and also produces the dashed negative amenity connection to utility. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4, waste/capacity branches]]

Read $W<A$ as waste remaining below the capacity represented in this schematic model, and $W>A$ as waste exceeding it. The latter case makes the feedback explicit: undesirable output can impair the environmental resource base and reduce utility. As with harvesting and growth, the comparison requires a common basis of measurement. The slide gives no units or detailed physical law and does not discuss the equality case $W=A$. It also does not establish that all waste below capacity is harmless in every setting. The diagram's positive and negative arrows represent its qualitative framework, not a universal empirical emissions rule. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4]]

### Several paths to wellbeing

Consumption has a positive dashed link to utility. Natural resources also connect to utility through the upper “Positive amenity (+)” path, while waste exceeding capacity connects through the lower-right “Negative amenity (−)” path. These distinct paths show why production or consumption alone cannot describe the whole environment–economy relationship: the same network contains benefits from consumption, benefits from environmental amenities, and losses associated with environmental pressures. This is an explanatory reading of the diagram, not a quantitative welfare formula. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4]]

These distinct paths show why production or consumption alone cannot describe the whole environment–economy relationship: the same network contains benefits from consumption, benefits from environmental amenities, and losses associated with environmental pressures. This is an explanatory reading of the diagram, not a quantitative welfare formula. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 4]]

## The economic questions placed on the network

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Intro_Slide_05_Economic_Questions.png]]

*The same network with the source's topic labels: resources, growth and sustainability, externality, regulation, and valuation. Reproduced from 00_Intro.pptx, slide 5. The placement connects each topic to the physical or utility relationships it concerns.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 5]]

Slide 5 overlays the course's economic questions on the physical network. **Resources** appears beside the resource branches. **Growth and sustainability** appears above the production-and-consumption relationship. **Externality** appears along feedback paths. **Regulation** appears around the production/waste part of the network. **Valuation** appears beside the amenity connections to utility. The overlay locates these topics but does not derive a policy instrument, an optimal pollution level, a valuation formula or a growth model. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 5]]

An explanatory synthesis is to use this network as a sequence of questions. What resources support economic activity? Does resource use outrun replenishment? How much waste reaches the environment relative to its capacity? Which pathways change wellbeing, and how should those changes be assessed? The source's regulation and valuation labels point toward these policy and assessment questions. Formal externality theory and instrument comparisons belong to later material and are not supplied by these introductory diagrams. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 4–6]]

source_units.heading: What the introductory framework establishes
source_units.text:
## What the introductory framework establishes

The economy depends on resources and wider environmental services, while production and consumption generate waste and feedback to the environment and utility. The crucial conditions in the source diagram compare harvest with growth and waste with assimilative capacity. These conditions make resource renewal and environmental capacity part of the analysis. The diagram offers a conceptual foundation for later policy assessment, while leaving quantitative models, measurements and climate science unspecified. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 2–5]]

The [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Course_Orientation_and_Week_1_Scope#Week 1 content supplied and content only advertised|scope note]] identifies the separate climate-foundation lecture referenced on slide 1. The uploaded deck supplies the environment–economy introduction, rather than the physical climate mechanisms, mitigation/adaptation/geoengineering explanations, or Kyoto-to-Paris history advertised for that lecture.

# Course Orientation and Week 1 Scope

What will Economics of Green Deal examine, and what does the first week's uploaded material actually explain? The course studies environmental problems and climate change through economics, including how optimal regulation is defined and how policies' economic, social and environmental impacts can be quantified. It gives special attention to decarbonisation scenarios and pathways, technology and social innovation. This note records that orientation and the assessment information, while identifying which Week 1 topics are supported by the supplied files. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=1|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1, English annotation and aim]]

Course navigation: [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Economics_of_Green_Deal_main#Week 1|Economics of Green Deal — Week 1]]. The [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Environment_Economy_Nexus|Environment–Economy Nexus]] note explains the substantive introductory diagrams.

## Údaje o předmětu v dodaném SIS exportu

Dodaný export SIS označuje předmět jako **Economics of Green Deal — JEB159**. Uvádí zimní semestr, 5 E-kreditů, výuku v angličtině, prezenční formu a písemnou zkoušku. Prerekvizitou je **JEB104**. Garantem je Mgr. Milan Ščasný, Ph.D. Tyto údaje pocházejí z české části exportu; nejsou nově ověřeným živým rozvrhem. Složka kurzu zůstává Economics_of_Green_Deal, podle existující struktury trezoru. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=1|Předměty.pdf, fyzická strana PDF 1, údaje o předmětu]]

Hlavička exportu uvádí akademický rok **2026/2027**, ale anglické popisy a sylabus nesou datum poslední úpravy **29.09.2025**. Přednášky v podkladech používají data 29. září, 6. října atd., zatímco slide 9 uvádí pondělní výuku. Podklady tak nelze bez dalšího použít jako potvrzený kalendář pro rok 2026/2027. Data v tomto zápisu jsou označení ze zdrojů, nikoli nově vytvořený rozvrh. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=1|Předměty.pdf, fyzická strana PDF 1, hlavička a datum úpravy]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=2|Předměty.pdf, fyzická strana PDF 2, sylabus]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 6 and 9]]

## The course's central question

The English annotation frames the European Green Deal as a policy to transform the EU into a carbon-neutral, resource-efficient and competitive economy. The transition involves technology, behaviour and lifestyle, and the course asks how to assess its impacts on the economy, environment and people. Environmental economics supplies the foundation, complemented by energy, transport and behavioural economics, energy-system modelling and environmental sciences. These are the course's stated aims and framing, rather than separately verified claims about current policy outcomes. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=1|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1, English annotation]]

The introductory [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Environment_Economy_Nexus|environment–economy framework]] explains why that assessment has several dimensions. Resources and environmental services support economic activity, waste feeds back into the environment, and both consumption and environmental amenities affect utility. Consequently, the course's stated environmental, economic and social impact questions share a common conceptual setting. This connection is a synthesis of the annotation and the introductory diagrams. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 2–5]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=1|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1]]

## Week 1 content supplied and content only advertised

The Week 1 lecture is titled **“Setting the Stage — Climate Change: Physical Foundation and Policy Implications”**, attributed to Miroslav Havránek, CENIA and Charles University Environment Center. The source labels it September 29. The SIS syllabus advertises two strands: mitigation, adaptation, a global perspective and geoengineering solutions; and the historical context from Kyoto to Paris to the Green Deal. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 1 and 6]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=2|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2, Week 1 syllabus]]

The uploaded 00_Intro.pptx contains ten slides. Slides 2–5 explain environmental functions and the environment–economy network. Slides 6–8 give the course schedule, and slides 9–10 give contacts, materials and assessment information. Slide 1 contains the climate-foundation lecture title and a hyperlink to a Prezi presentation; the climate-foundation presentation itself is not embedded in the uploaded file. No hidden slide or substantive speaker note supplies that missing content. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 1–10]]

**Source limitation:** the supplied files identify the climate-foundation topics but do not explain their physical mechanisms, evidence, history, or policy details. Those strands remain advertised topics, rather than completed teaching coverage. The linked Prezi was not accessed in this ingestion, and no explanation was invented from the title or syllabus bullets. An accessible copy of that lecture would be needed to ingest those strands in full. The uploaded introduction and Week 1 SIS information are covered here. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 1]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=2|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2]]

The SIS document also describes Weeks 2–12 and lists other downloadable materials. These regions were inspected to establish their scope, but their academic content is excluded from this Week 1 ingestion. In particular, this note does not cover the Week 2 readings, policy-instrument comparisons, later modelling lectures, or later distributional and behavioural topics. The schedule slides provide orientation only. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slides 6–8]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=2|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2, Week 2–5 syllabus]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=3|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 3, Week 6–12 syllabus]]

## Assessment and grading in the supplied materials

The deck and SIS export agree on three components. A writing test with a satisfactory grade carries **65 points**, the written open-book examination carries **35 points**, and active participation in lectures carries **10 points**. The open-book exam is described as testing understanding and application rather than memorisation. The source qualifies permitted material as “all, but electronic,” which excludes electronic materials under its stated wording. It does not enumerate particular permitted paper resources. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 10]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=2|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2, completion requirements]]

| Points stated in the source | Grade |
|---|---|
| 91 and more | A |
| 81–90 | B |
| 71–80 | C |
| 61–70 | D |
| 51–60 | E |
| 50 and less | Failed |

These are point bands, not percentages. The three displayed component allocations sum to 110 points. The supplied materials do not explain whether participation is a bonus, whether the final result is capped, or how fractional point totals would be handled. Keep the source's allocations and thresholds without inventing a normalization or a bonus rule. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 10]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=2|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2, grading]]

## Contacts and materials recorded in the deck

Slide 9 names Milan Ščasný as coordinator and supplies milan.scasny@czp.cuni.cz. It gives lectures as Mondays, 15:30–16:50, room O206, and identifies SIS as the materials location. Offices are listed at the Institute of Economic Studies (#408) and the Environment Center (José Martího 2/407, #1617). Office hours require prior communication, by email or after lectures. These are the deck's administrative statements, subject to the calendar limitation above. The deck labels the course JEB159, with JEM335 in parentheses, and prints “5 ETS”; the SIS export separately states 5 E-kreditů. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 9]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/Předměty.pdf#page=1|Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1]]

It also lists Miroslav Havránek (environmental sciences, CENIA/CUNI), Richard Juřík (Ministry of the Environment), and Vladimír Kubeček (ČEPS/TSO, VŠE). These roles provide orientation; their later subject matter is outside this Week 1 coverage. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_1/00_Intro.pptx|00_Intro.pptx, slide 9]]

source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Externalities_and_Welfare_Optimum.md#Identify the externality before proposing a remedy
source_units.text:
## Identify the externality before proposing a remedy

The chapter's definition has two actors: a **supplier** whose action determines a real variable and a **receptor** whose utility or production function depends on it. The supplier does not account for that effect in choosing the action. Noise, contaminated water or air quality can be such real variables. An upstream factory that discharges waste, reduces dissolved oxygen and fish stocks, and harms downstream anglers illustrates the mechanism. If downstream welfare does not enter the factory's decision, the private return from production remains higher than its social return. The lecture also presents the uncompensated-welfare-loss wording of an external cost. The definition used in the chapter makes the neglected real relationship central; compensation and incentives require separate analysis. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=3|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 3,5–6]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=3|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3,5]]

A physical environmental change without a utility or production consequence does not establish an economic externality. An unpriced relationship is also insufficient. Barter can exchange benefits implicitly, and altruism deliberately takes another person's pleasure into account. The chapter excludes deliberate violence, jealousy and promotion from its externality category as well. This is a classification of the argument for efficiency correction, not approval of harmful conduct or a claim that policy has no equity or other rationale. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=7|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 7–10]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=3|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 3]]

**Pecuniary effects** operate through prices in existing markets. A change in transport or input prices moves a consumer along a given demand/utility relationship rather than creating the technological shift represented by an externality. Under the competitive assumptions here, the market already transmits these effects. Greater consumer surplus from cheaper output can be valuable without being an external benefit. Employment and value added in related industries are likewise not evidence that excessive externality-generating activity should be encouraged. Infrastructure investment and the actual use of infrastructure need separate assessments. The [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Road_Transport_External_Costs|transport note]] develops these distinctions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=9|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 9–10,19]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=3|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3–5]]

### Types and boundaries

Positive versus negative refers to the receptor's benefit or loss, while production versus consumption refers to the originating activity. Spatial neighbourhood, partial/global and intergenerational classifications identify the reach of the effect. The lecture also lists effects involving several interacting uses, such as fishing, boating and swimming, and marginal versus inframarginal effects. These classifications identify which relationships require measurement; the lecture supplies no separate formal model for every category. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=12|Lecture, physical PDF p. 12]]

A **depletable** effect differs from an **undepletable** effect in whether one receptor's consumption changes what is available to others. An undepletable externality has public-good or public-bad characteristics alongside the externality. The chapter reports that this distinction does not require different Pigouvian pricing rules by itself, but can make voluntary bargaining vulnerable to strategic behaviour and free riding. In **congestion**, an actor can simultaneously cause and receive effects; the appropriate individual-level incentive does not disappear merely because the harm stays inside the road-user sector. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=3|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3,6–7]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=12|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 12,27]]

source_units.heading: What welfare criteria can establish
source_units.text:
## What welfare criteria can establish

A **Pareto improvement** makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off. A **Pareto-efficient allocation** leaves no feasible rearrangement that everyone weakly prefers, with somebody strictly preferring it. These criteria make relatively little use of interpersonal welfare comparisons, but they cannot rank alternative efficient allocations with different distributions. Verhoef contrasts them with **potential Pareto** or compensation criteria: the winners could compensate the losers so that a Pareto improvement becomes possible. The Kaldor criterion accepts the change if its winners could compensate its losers afterwards. The Hicks criterion accepts it if the initial losers could not compensate the winners sufficiently to prevent the change. These are differently directed compensation tests, not a requirement that a transfer actually occurs. Actual compensation is not required by the potential criterion. Therefore a positive aggregate net benefit can coexist with people who lose. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=2|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 2]]

Under the conditions of the first welfare theorem, a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient; the second theorem relates alternative efficient allocations to appropriate endowment distributions. The chapter also relates maxima of Paretian, welfaristic social welfare functions to efficiency and, under concavity, the converse with suitable welfare weights. These are conditional results. Increasing returns, market power, external effects, public goods and imperfect information can prevent their usual competitive conclusion. Equity and merit-good arguments are additional rationales for intervention, distinct from a demonstration of market failure. A failure identifies a possible efficiency rationale; an intervention still needs gains exceeding its costs. The chapter calls a technological externality potentially Pareto relevant when correcting it costs less than the available welfare gain. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=2|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 2–3]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=4|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 4,22]]

## The next-chapter fragment included in the file

Physical PDF p. 10 includes printed p. 215, the opening of “Endogenous environmental risk” by Crocker and Shogren. It defines risk through an event's likelihood and severity and explains how defensive choices can alter these, particularly when insurance/contingent-claims markets are incomplete. Examples include boiling contaminated drinking water, filtering water, changing outdoor activity and using sunscreen. Insurance compensates an insured loss; it does not by itself change the probability. Defining only contamination as a fixed state can hide the household's ability to change the risk of illness through boiling. This is an additional supplied fragment, not the full chapter, and contains no complete risk model or later argument to reconstruct. source_units.heading: What to retain
source_units.text:
## What to retain

Identify a neglected real welfare relationship before applying externality policy. In the smooth first-best model, compare social marginal benefit and social marginal cost; optimal damage can remain positive. Compensation, internalization and regulation have different incentive and distribution effects. The efficiency optimum is conditional and cannot by itself settle fairness, income-sensitive valuation or political feasibility. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=3|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3–9]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=20|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 20–28]]

source_units.heading: Derive the private and social activity levels
source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Externalities_and_Welfare_Optimum.md#Derive the private and social activity levels
source_units.text:
## Derive the private and social activity levels

Let $Q$ denote an activity level over a given period, $MPB(Q)$ marginal private benefit, $MPC(Q)$ marginal private cost, $MEC(Q)$ marginal external cost and $MEB(Q)$ marginal external benefit. Marginal quantities are money or welfare equivalents per unit of $Q$, measured on a common basis. In the source's smooth partial-equilibrium diagrams, private choice satisfies

$$MPB(Q^0)=MPC(Q^0).$$

Without external effects this also maximizes the area between the benefit and cost curves. With negative external effects,

$$MSC(Q)=MPC(Q)+MEC(Q),\qquad MPB(Q^*)=MPC(Q^*)+MEC(Q^*).$$

An explanatory mathematical reconstruction of the diagram is

$$W(Q)=\int_0^Q\big[MPB(q)-MPC(q)-MEC(q)\big]dq,$$

so that $W'(Q)=MPB(Q)-MPC(Q)-MEC(Q)$. The interior optimum sets this derivative to zero; a negative second derivative or suitable concavity is needed for a maximum. The source's increasing marginal external cost and decreasing net private benefit produce $Q^*<Q^0$. This formula is a synthesis of the source's areas, rather than an extra empirical model. It excludes other distortions and any fixed costs absent from the diagram. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=3|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3–5,9 note7]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=14|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 14–15,20]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week2_Externality_Optimum_Slide15.png]]

*Lecture physical PDF p. 15: the downward curve is marginal net private benefit ($MNPB=MPB-MPC$), the upward curve is MEC. At zero activity, the diagram normalizes welfare to zero. At unrestricted $Q_{max}$, private net benefit is $A+B+C$ and damage is $B+C+D$, giving $A-D$. At $Q_{optimum}$, private net benefit is $A+B$, damage is $B$, and welfare is $A$. The increase from restriction is $D$, while $B$ remains as optimal damage.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=15|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 15,25]]

The lettered areas in this lecture figure differ from those in Verhoef's Figure 13.1. In the chapter's negative-externality panel, $A$ denotes optimal external damage and $C$ the deadweight loss avoided by restricting activity. Area labels must always be read within their own figure. Optimization does **not** imply eliminating all external damage. Nor is reducing production necessarily a strict Pareto improvement: the supplier loses private returns and would need appropriate compensation to satisfy that stronger criterion. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=4|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 4–5]]

For a positive externality, social benefit is $MSB=MPB+MEB$ and the condition is

$$MPB(Q^*)+MEB(Q^*)=MPC(Q^*).$$

The source's diagrams imply $Q^*>Q^0$: the supplier otherwise omits part of the benefit. A correcting subsidy $s^*=MEB(Q^*)$ can align the private choice, just as $t^*=MEC(Q^*)$ can correct the negative externality in the simple setting. These are marginal, optimum-specific rates, not total damage divided arbitrarily by output. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=16|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 16–20]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=4|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 4–5]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week2_Positive_Externality_Slide17.png]]

*Lecture p. 17: adding the external benefit raises MSB above MPB, moves the chosen output from $Q^0$ toward $Q^*$ and supplies the subsidy wedge $s^*$.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=17|Lecture, physical PDF p. 17]]

The lecture p. 18 compares output below, at and above $Q^*$ using coloured areas. Its line for $Q^+>Q^*$ adds the pointwise expression $MSB[q^+]-MPC[q^+]$ to areas $A+B+C$. A marginal value and a total welfare area have different dimensions; that printed expression should not be used as a complete total-welfare identity. The reliable comparison follows the marginal curves: beyond their intersection the extra activity has negative marginal social surplus, so its accumulated welfare effect is the integral of that negative difference. This dimensional clarification is agent synthesis of the diagram and the chapter's area definition. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=18|Lecture, physical PDF p. 18]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=3|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3–5]]

### Why a cost reduction is not a new external benefit

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week2_Verhoef2002_Figure13_1.png]]

*Verhoef physical p. 4, printed pp. 202–203, Figure 13.1: normal market choice, negative external cost, positive external benefit and pecuniary benefit. The original spread has been rotated for readability.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=4|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 4]]

In panel (d), a lower private cost curve lowers social cost too, assuming the external cost function is unchanged. The new efficient output can increase, and lower market prices increase consumer surplus through a movement along MPB. That price-mediated benefit is pecuniary. The external wedge remains: new unrestricted output still exceeds the new optimum. Calling the extra consumer surplus an external benefit would wrongly suggest another subsidy on top of the remaining correction. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=4|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 4–5]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=19|Lecture, physical PDF p. 19]]

source_units.heading: Four different policy concepts
source_units.text:
## Four different policy concepts

**Optimization** means choosing an effect level consistent with optimal allocation under the potential Pareto criterion. **Compensation** is a transfer covering the receptor's welfare effect. **Internalization**, in the chapter's narrow terminology, removes the external character by creating a market for the effect or gathering interests, for example by merging an upstream and a downstream firm. **Regulation** is direct government intervention, including taxes, standards or permits. The chapter explicitly notes that Pigouvian taxation is often called internalization in broader usage, although it does not create a market and thus fails its narrow definition. The lecture uses both regulation and market creation in explaining remedies. Preserve that terminology difference rather than equating all four operations. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=5|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 5,9 note9]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=28|Lecture, physical PDF p. 28]]

A transfer need not optimize behaviour. If receptors are automatically reimbursed for residual harm or protective spending, they may have less reason to choose efficient defensive measures. Conversely, a negotiated payment under well-defined rights can coexist with efficient choice because the bargain itself governs the effect. The [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Road_Transport_External_Costs#Activity abatement and defence are jointly chosen|abatement-and-defence model]] shows why incentives at both sides matter. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=5|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 5–6]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=28|Lecture, physical PDF p. 28]]

source_units.heading: Coasean bargaining and its limitations
source_units.text:
## Coasean bargaining and its limitations

The lecture illustrates bargaining with radio stations whose broadcasts interfere. With enforceable rights, transferable money, feasible ways of avoiding the harm and no transaction costs, the station with the higher-valued use can compensate the other to obtain that use. In the usual Coasean argument, bargaining reaches an efficient outcome regardless of initial rights, under the stated ideal conditions and with the lecture's uniqueness qualification. Initial rights still govern who pays whom and how surplus is distributed. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=23|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 23–24]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=3|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3,7–8]]

Transaction costs include finding and coordinating participants, negotiating, monitoring and enforcing agreements. The lecture's factory facing a thousand landowners illustrates why the two-person ideal becomes difficult: individual victims can wait for others to finance the improvement. Missing environmental-quality rights and undepletable public-bad effects add difficulties. With transaction costs, the attainable allocation can depend on initial rights. The lecture's “Second Coase theorem” recommends institutions that reduce reallocation costs, while admitting that governments cannot know the highest-valued use without cost. This title is the lecture's wording, not a reason to omit its qualifications. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=26|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 26–27]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=3|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 3]]

source_units.heading: Efficiency and equity lead to different comparisons
source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Externalities_and_Welfare_Optimum.md#Efficiency and equity lead to different comparisons
source_units.text:
## Efficiency and equity lead to different comparisons

An efficient tax sets the marginal incentive; it need not equal the total unpaid bill. For an increasing MEC curve, the rectangle $Q^*t^*$ can exceed the area of total external damage. In the chapter's linear diagram it is twice the optimal external damage $A$. With constant MEC, marginal and average damage coincide. Thus the polluter-pays principle is ambiguous until one specifies payment of total damage, marginal incentive, or both. Willingness to pay or accept also depends on income: the same physical exposure can receive a larger money valuation for a richer receptor. Locating pollution where measured money damage is low can therefore conflict with equity concerns. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=6|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 6]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week2_Verhoef2002_Table13_1.png]]

*Table 13.1, physical p. 7, printed p. 208. The efficiency question needs marginal external cost, individual aggregation and both intra- and intersectoral harm. The unpaid-bill question needs total external cost plus defensive outlays, sectoral aggregation and costs shifted outside the sector. Footnotes retain the qualifications on insurance and taxes.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=7|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 7]]

A fixed annual insurance premium or ownership tax has little direct effect on the next kilometre driven. It can nevertheless matter to unpaid-bill accounting, with the table's restrictions: insurance payments must be compared with costs imposed outside the sector; ownership taxes cover unpaid costs only above infrastructure expenditure; fuel taxes used as Pigouvian corrections need a differential above ordinary indirect taxation, apart from second-best taxation questions. Existing transfers should therefore be evaluated against the actual research question. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=7|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 7]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week2_Verhoef2002_Figure13_2.png]]

*Figure 13.2, physical p. 7, printed p. 209. Its letters belong to this figure, separately from Figure 13.1 and the lecture diagram.* Here $MNPB=MPB-MPC$ is marginal net private benefit in money per unit of activity $Q$, and $MEC$ is marginal external cost in the same units. The private choice $Q^0$ has $MNPB=0$; the social choice $Q^*$ has $MNPB=MEC=t^*$. The labelled areas integrate these marginal quantities and therefore measure money, rather than money per unit. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=7|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 7]]

To read the letters, start left of $Q^*$. Area $A$ lies between $MNPB$ and the horizontal tax level $t^*$; $B$ lies between $t^*$ and $MEC$; $C$ is below $MEC$. Thus net private benefit through $Q^*$ is $A+B+C$, damage is $C$, the tax rectangle is $B+C$, and social welfare is $A+B$. Right of $Q^*$, $D$ is below $MNPB$ between $Q^*$ and $Q^0$, while $E$ is between $MEC$ and $MNPB$. Continuing to $Q^0$ adds private benefit $D$ and damage $D+E$, lowering social welfare by $E$. Unrestricted private benefit is consequently $A+B+C+D$, damage is $C+D+E$, and their difference is $A+B-E$. This construction makes every transfer in Table 13.2 interpretable without borrowing another diagram's letters. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=7|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 7–8]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week2_Verhoef2002_Table13_2.png]]

*Table 13.2, physical p. 8, printed p. 210. It compares distribution under a single producer, a single victim unable to defend itself, and the Figure 13.2 area convention. Parentheses denote transfers between producer and victim; square brackets denote transfers to the regulator. In the simple model all optimizing schemes yield social welfare $A+B$, while non-intervention yields $A+B-E$.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=7|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 7–8]]

A quantity restriction leaves producer welfare $A+B+C$ and victim welfare $-C$. A Pigouvian tax transfers $B+C$ to the regulator, leaving producer welfare $A$, victim welfare $-C$ and the same social total. Direct compensation transfers $C$ to the victim, leaving it at zero and the producer at $A+B$. A merger gathers the interests into the common total. If the producer owns the right, the victim pays to reduce production: the two extreme-bargainer cases transfer $D$ or $D+E$ and leave the producer above its unrestricted welfare in one case. If the victim owns the right, the producer pays between $C$ and $A+B+C$ in the table's extreme cases. The upper payment $D+E$ assumes truthful bargaining: chapter note 12 excludes a producer threatening output above the private choice $Q^0$ to extract a larger payment. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=9|Verhoef Externalities, physical p. 9, printed p. 213, note 12]] These are alternative distributional bounds, not simultaneous payments. The chapter consequently explains why producer and victim rank schemes differently and why political support for standards can differ from support for taxes. Revenue allocation is assumed ignored by both actors in the table's tax row. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=7|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 7–8]]

The tax-versus-quantity equivalence here relies on a deliberately simple model. Chapter note 8 warns that uncertainty and heterogeneity can break it; tradable permits also introduce a market absent from a plain quantity restriction. The [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Market_Based_Environmental_Instruments|instrument note]] explains cost effectiveness and enforcement, while the [[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Optimal_Environmental_Taxation|taxation note]] adds pre-existing fiscal distortions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01a_Verhoef_2002-1.pdf#page=9|Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 9 notes8,11]] [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/01_Regulation_Externality-1.pdf#page=31|Lecture, physical PDF pp. 31–54]]

source_units.heading: Activity abatement and defence are jointly chosen
source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Road_Transport_External_Costs.md#Activity abatement and defence are jointly chosen
source_units.text:
## Activity abatement and defence are jointly chosen

The basic output diagram makes harm depend only on $Q$. The richer model allows the supplier to reduce damage through **abatement** (for example quieter/cleaner vehicles) and the receptor to reduce exposure through **defensive measures** (for example double glazing). Let $Q$ be the externality-causing activity, $A$ monetary abatement outlays by the supplier, $D$ monetary defensive outlays by the victim, and $EC$ the residual or **net external cost** after those measures:

$$EC=EC(Q,D,A).$$

The article sometimes writes the argument order $(Q,A,D)$; variable names consistently identify the same three inputs. With $PC(Q)$ private production cost, the distinctions are

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{gross private cost}&=PC(Q)+A,\\
\text{gross external cost}&=EC(Q,D,A)+D,\\
\text{social cost of the activity}&=PC(Q)+A+EC(Q,D,A)+D.
\end{aligned}$$

Defensive expenditure consumes real resources even if it succeeds in reducing experienced harm. Ignoring it treats an externally induced expense as costless. Abatement is included on the supplier's side rather than being added automatically to the receptor's unpaid bill. The article cautions that this explicit supplier/victim split fits environmental nuisance better than congestion or accidents, where the same road user can be on both sides. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=6|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 6, equation1 and footnote5]]

### Assumptions and derivative notation

A subscript denotes a partial derivative holding the other arguments fixed: $EC_Q=\partial EC/\partial Q$, $EC_{DD}=\partial^2 EC/\partial D^2$, and so forth. The paper assumes

$$EC_Q>0,\quad EC_{QQ}\geq0;\qquad EC_D<0,\quad EC_{DD}>0;\qquad EC_A<0,\quad EC_{AA}>0.$$

Activity raises residual damage at a nondecreasing marginal rate. Spending on defence or abatement reduces it, but each additional money unit has diminishing damage-reduction effectiveness. For smooth functions it also postulates

$$EC_{DQ}=EC_{QD}<0,\qquad EC_{AQ}=EC_{QA}<0,\qquad EC_{AD}=EC_{DA}>0.$$

More activity gives protective outlays more damage to reduce; protection lowers the damage added by extra activity. The positive cross derivative between $A$ and $D$ means greater protection on one side reduces the marginal effectiveness of the other side. These are assumed functional properties for the model's likely case, not measured transport coefficients. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=7|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 7, equations2a–i]]

Let $PB(Q)$ be private benefit and define net private benefit as $NPB(Q)=PB(Q)-PC(Q)$. The displayed equation makes this a difference, although the source's adjacent prose mistakenly calls it a “sum”; the subtraction is also used in its welfare function. The assumption $NPB_{QQ}<0$ means diminishing marginal net private benefit. Supplier welfare and victim welfare are

$$W^p=NPB(Q)-A,\qquad W^v=-EC(Q,D,A)-D.$$

Summing them gives

$$W=NPB(Q)-EC(Q,D,A)-A-D.$$

The monetary units of $A$ and $D$ are crucial: a one-unit increase directly costs one unit of welfare in this money-valued representation. The model's additive welfare measure abstracts from additional income effects or heterogeneous welfare weights. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=7|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 7, equations3–6]]

### Derive and interpret the efficient conditions

Differentiate the welfare expression with respect to each choice:

$$\begin{aligned}
W_Q&=NPB_Q-EC_Q=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad NPB_Q=EC_Q,\\
W_A&=-EC_A-1=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad EC_A=-1,\\
W_D&=-EC_D-1=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad EC_D=-1.
\end{aligned}$$

The first condition balances the benefit sacrificed by reducing activity against the avoided damage. The second and third say that a last money unit spent on either abatement or defence avoids one money unit of residual harm. Together, all three available ways of reducing external cost have the same marginal efficiency. They apply to an interior solution. Boundary constraints can instead prevent an equality, and the paper's footnote7 requires the relevant Hessian conditions for a welfare maximum; stationarity alone is insufficient. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=7|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 7–8, equations7a–c]]

Without a mechanism making residual damage enter the supplier's objective, it chooses $Q$ to maximize $NPB$ and has no benefit from $A$ in $W^p$, so the simple model predicts excessive activity and zero abatement. A victim who bears both damage and protective cost already faces the $D$ tradeoff and can behave efficiently on that margin. Automatic compensation can alter this incentive. This motivates policies aimed first at reducing activity and inducing abatement, while examining what compensation does to defence. It is a result of the model's separation of objectives, not a universal prediction that every real driver makes no voluntary abatement investment. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=8|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 8]]

Minimizing the activity's social **cost** alone would select no activity and no outlays, whereas maximizing welfare balances costs against benefits. The paper contrasts this with a nuisance-based cost convention including foregone production: different definitions can make a “minimum social cost” statement mean a different optimization problem. Always identify the accounting boundary before using that phrase. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=8|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 8, footnote8]]

source_units.heading: Transport benefits and external benefits are different
source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Road_Transport_External_Costs.md#Transport benefits and external benefits are different
source_units.text:
## Transport benefits and external benefits are different

The article requires a real variable in a receptor's utility/profit function whose value depends on a supplier's behaviour and is omitted from that supplier's decision. Ordinary economic dependencies through prices are excluded from this definition. In the paper's simple Figure 1, external costs push unrestricted activity beyond its efficient level, while external benefits would justify encouragement. A downward private-cost shift can increase consumer surplus while leaving the external-cost wedge intact. Thus useful transport and technological external benefit are different propositions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=2|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 2–3]]

The author finds no significant external benefits of **individual road transport activities**, apart from a possible car-spotter example. Cheaper production, wider product choice and faster delivery generally enter market transactions; associated employment and value added do not justify transport above its optimum. Visits to friends can reflect reciprocal exchange or deliberate altruism. Infrastructure's contribution to accessibility and regional development belongs to the investment appraisal, rather than being credited as an external benefit of each extra trip. Better emergency access also depends on infrastructure; more traffic may instead obstruct it through congestion. These conclusions are the author's classifications under the stated market framework, including the assumption of no distortions elsewhere when tracing market benefits to final consumers. They do not say transport has no private or social benefit. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=4|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 4–6]]

### Classify the harm and its incidence

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week2_Verhoef1994_Transport_Typology.png]]

*Figure 2, physical PDF p. 4 (printed p. 276), also reproduced in lecture p. 11. Rows separate intra-sectoral harm among road users from ecological and social environmental harm; columns separate moving traffic, stationary vehicles and infrastructure-associated effects. Shading represents first-order incidence.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=4|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 4]]

Congestion lies largely within the sector; noise affects social surroundings; air, water and soil pollution reach ecological surroundings; accidents have several incidences, including fellow road users and people outside the sector, and hazardous-material accidents can harm ecosystems. Parking consumes public space and can create parking congestion. Infrastructure can sever biotopes, create visual annoyance or impose barriers within communities. The article displays this broad typology but explicitly excludes environmental effects caused by the mere presence of infrastructure from its later analysis. A second-order effect can connect categories: congestion increases emissions per vehicle-kilometre. Severity is sensitive to time and place. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=4|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 4, footnote2]]

source_units.heading: Efficiency and the unpaid bill require different measures
source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/Road_Transport_External_Costs.md#Efficiency and the unpaid bill require different measures
source_units.text:
## Efficiency and the unpaid bill require different measures

One question asks for optimal marginal choices or road prices. The other asks what total burden transport shifts to other people. The second requires $EC+D$, rather than residual damage alone. Average gross burden indicates an optimal marginal rate only under additional conditions such as constant marginal external cost; total harm divided by total kilometres generally does not supply a time-and-place-specific optimal price. There is no single aggregate optimal road-transport quantity independent of location and time. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=8|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 8]]

The level of aggregation matters too. Harm imposed by one motorist on another is external to the first motorist but remains inside the motorist sector. Adding that harm to environmental damage can be appropriate for some social-cost questions, but it cannot be labelled without qualification as the sector's unpaid bill to the rest of society. This distinction becomes especially important in accident accounting. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=8|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 8–9]]

source_units.heading: Accidents: risk valuation and aggregation
source_units.text:
## Accidents: risk valuation and aggregation

Accident costs can include vehicle/property/environmental damage, legal/police/emergency costs, medical/funeral costs, pain and suffering and lost production. Responsibility can be shared in a chain collision; a responsible driver's own injury can impose further losses on relatives and society. Some published studies define social accident costs as total costs less insurance coverage, which differs from the article's earlier total private-plus-external social-cost definition. Fixed yearly insurance premiums can compensate losses without pricing the marginal kilometre, so compensation does not establish optimized accident risk. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=12|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 12–13, footnote12]]

Valuing life solely through expected net production can give negative values for elderly or jobless people. The author instead favours ex ante valuation of changes in physical risk. Historical estimates differ substantially by concept: the paper cites ECU 12,280 for gross earnings in Portugal, ECU 1,667,246 for social willingness to pay in Switzerland, and an even lower Netherlands friction-cost estimate of DFL 2,400 (about ECU 1,000). These are evidence of incompatible valuation concepts rather than comparable prices of a human being. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=13|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 13–14]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week2_Verhoef1994_Table3_Accidents.png]]

*Table 3, PDF p. 13, printed p. 285. The original source clips some text at the right margin; the legible numerical columns and method distinctions are retained. These are social accident costs with varied boundaries, not one consistently defined environmental external-cost series.* [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=13|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 13]]

The Swiss Neuenschwander et al. (1991) rows give SF 5,379 million / 1.70% GDP in social costs, SF 1,488 million / 0.47% GDP in external cost at individual level, and SF 789 million / 0.25% GDP at mode level. The footnote on PDF p. 12 likewise contrasts individual and mode aggregation for car traffic and reports a larger proportional reduction for rail traffic. Changing the analytical boundary changes what is external. The paper therefore warns against adding these accident totals to noise and air-pollution external costs and calling the result transport's external burden. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_2/ARTICLE_01b_Verhoef_1994.pdf#page=12|Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 12 footnote11,13–14]]
