It connects the method to DPSIR: driving forces, pressures, state, impacts and responses. Its note that “I” is monetized impacts describes the valuation endpoint of this application; one must still calculate physical impacts before money values can be attached. Damage depends on technology, operation, location, time, the included fuel-cycle boundary and population preferences. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=3|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 3–4]]

source_units.heading: From concentration to a receptor-specific impact
source_units.text:
## From concentration to a receptor-specific impact

The Lauffen/Stuttgart example maps changes in sulfate concentration due to a plant's SO2 emissions across Europe. The pressure-map legend is in **ng/m³**. A separate receptor map shows where potentially exposed people live. The mortality/life-year-loss map combines exposure changes and population response: a high concentration change in a sparsely populated area need not create the largest health loss. Transboundary transport explains why damages need not stay within the emitting jurisdiction. The maps' different units and colour breaks must not be equated. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=5|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 5–8]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Impact_Pathway.png]]

The source diagram moves from emissions through transport/chemistry to human/material/crop effects and only then money. Treating an emission quantity itself as a welfare loss would skip the receptor and valuation steps. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=5|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 5]]

An exposure/dose/concentration-response function connects a specified exposure change with a specified outcome. Physical p. 9 gives the illustrative equation

$$\text{additional years of life lost}=3.9\times10^{-5}\,\Delta\text{Sulfate}\times\text{Population}.$$

The coefficient embodies a response per concentration unit and exposed person, so concentration units, population definition and exposure period must match its calibration. The slide does **not** supply those calibration units/time details; the ng/m³ map is not permission to assume the equation uses ng/m³. This formula supports the pathway logic, but not a reproducible numerical health estimate without that missing context. Its graph contrasts linear, nonlinear, threshold/limited and initially beneficial (“fertilizing”) shapes; choosing a straight line is a substantive response assumption, not an automatic property of every pollutant. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=9|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 9]]

source_units.heading: Endpoints and the source response-value table
source_units.text:
## Endpoints and the source response-value table

The source includes particulate matter, SO2/NOx/NH3/VOC, CO2, heavy metals, noise and odour as burdens, with health, buildings/materials, crops, climate, landscape, visibility and cultural heritage as impact categories. Its p. 11 embedded comment adds respiratory admissions, restricted activity, congestive heart failure, nonfatal cancer, bronchitis and asthma; material ageing/soiling across metals, paint and stone; and crop-yield changes for barley, oats, potato, rye, sugar beet, wheat, sunflower, rice and tobacco. The category list does not assert that every burden affects every endpoint equally. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=11|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 11, 11]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Concentration_Response_Table.png]]

Physical p. 10's complete table retains its endpoint units and numerical entries. Long-term PM2.5 adult mortality is expressed per year of life lost (YOLL), while infant mortality and bronchitis rows are per case. Short-term PM2.5/PM10/O3 rows distinguish restricted/work days, respiratory/cardiovascular admissions, asthma symptoms and mortality. A value per day cannot be multiplied by a number of people without specifying days per person; a value per YOLL is not a value per death. The CRF column is calibrated per 10 µg/m³, whereas the noise rows use weighted day-evening-night level $L_{den}$ in dB and separate quadratic annoyance functions. The table alone does not supply baseline disease frequencies, age structure or valid concentration/noise ranges; do not extrapolate its curves outside their study context. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=10|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 10]]

A CRF such as **1.019 per 10 µg/m³** is a relative risk: for that concentration increment, the respiratory-admission rate is multiplied by 1.019, a **1.9% relative increase**. It is not 1.019 extra admissions per person, and it is not a YOLL conversion. As an explicitly simplified calculation for a 10 µg/m³ increase from a reference exposure, if the baseline admission rate is $r_0$ cases per person per year and the exposed population is $N$, then

$$\Delta\text{cases}\approx N r_0(1.019-1).$$

For an illustrative baseline of 0.01 admissions per person per year and 100,000 exposed people, the reference count is 1,000 admissions per year and the increase is 19 per year. These invented round inputs teach the calculation; they are not an estimate for the lecture's plant. Other increments require the study's specified response function, and reductions from an already exposed observed baseline require the corresponding attributable-fraction calculation rather than silently reusing the same baseline. The baseline incidence, exposed population, period and endpoint must match. Mortality-to-YOLL estimation additionally needs life-expectancy/age information; a relative-risk coefficient alone cannot produce life years. This expands the source's pathway reasoning, supported by the manuscript's Methods/Table 1. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=10|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 10]]

**Bounded reference verification:** Máca, Melichar, Ščasný and Braun Kohlová (2017), “Valuing environmental health for informed policy-making,” *Reviews on Environmental Health* 32(1–2), 171–175, author manuscript physical pp. 3–5 (Methods/Table 1/perspectives), confirms that background population and incidence enter the assessment, and identifies the values as euro 2014. It also distinguishes physical modeling uncertainty from economic standing/value choices. [Consulted author manuscript](https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/92550/1/MPRA_paper_92550.pdf). This verifies interpretation of the supplied table, rather than importing its whole case study as assigned scope.

source_units.heading: Monetizing the change in health and welfare
source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/Impact_Pathways_Health_Valuation_and_Standing.md#Monetizing the change in health and welfare
source_units.text:
## Monetizing the change in health and welfare

Market prices can inform crop losses, material repair and medical-resource costs. Non-market values address pain, premature mortality risk, recreation, aesthetic and landscape losses that have no complete market transaction. **Willingness to pay (WTP)** asks what someone would give up to avoid an adverse change or obtain an improvement. It is preference-based valuation of the change, not a statement that a person's intrinsic worth equals an invoice. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=12|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 12–13]]

For mortality, the source emphasizes WTP for a reduction in the risk of dying and the difficulty of eliciting life-expectancy changes. Quality-adjusted/disability-based values depend on context and cause; the lecture does not supply a universal price per QALY/DALY. For morbidity, cost of illness includes medical treatment and lost earnings, while pain/inconvenience require a separate welfare component. Development/fertility examples include risks of very low birth weight, birth defects, conception and IQ, plus IVF/training/earnings costs. Mental-health impacts can also be elicited through WTP studies. These components must be consistently defined to avoid counting the same loss twice. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=13|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 13]]

A useful **agent synthesis** of the pathway is

$$D=\sum_{r}\sum_{j}\Delta I_{rj}\,v_{rj},$$

where $\Delta I_{rj}$ is the modeled change in endpoint $j$ for receptor region $r$ and $v_{rj}$ is a value per matching endpoint unit, in a specified currency/year. This is not a new estimated response law: it states how checked physical changes and unit values combine. Changing receptor coverage or monetary weights changes $D$ even if emissions are unchanged. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=5|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 5, 10, 12–13, 19]]

source_units.heading: What the electricity comparisons show
source_units.text:
## What the electricity comparisons show

Physical p. 14 decomposes Czech plant external costs in Kč/kWh into health, crops, buildings, biodiversity and climate. Its plant totals differ, with the largest displayed bars around 3 Kč/kWh and smaller ones below 1; health is a major component. Physical p. 15 instead groups fuel/technology examples and explicitly states **2008 prices**: displayed examples range from about 0.2–0.4 for some gas configurations to 3.5 Kč/kWh for a biomass example; brown-coal examples include 1.2, 2.1, 2.9 and other values, and biogas examples 0.4, 0.5, 0.9. Different technologies and operating/location assumptions matter: the diagram is not proof that every biomass plant is more damaging than every coal plant. These are historical external-cost assessments, not current electricity prices or full private generation costs. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=14|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 14–15]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Electricity_External_Costs.png]]

The full fuel/technology graphic retains every category and displayed number. Its six-component legend includes heavy metals as well as health/biodiversity/climate/materials/crops. Read the bars within this source's price year and configuration labels; do not combine them with a current market tariff. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=15|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 15]]

source_units.heading: Denmark and local versus imported pollution
source_units.text:
## Denmark and local versus imported pollution

The 2021 Danish illustration attributes about 74% (roughly 3,000 premature deaths) to foreign sources and 26% (roughly 1,000) to Danish sources. Within the domestic pie it shows agriculture 22%, road traffic 21%, other mobile 7%, energy industries 7%, nonindustrial combustion 36%, others 7%; annotations include about 220 traffic deaths, about 70 each for other mobile/energy industries and about 330 household/SNAP2 deaths (about 240 from wood stoves). Danish contributions to deaths **abroad**, about 2,300, are a different receptor total. These rounded modeled source contributions are not additive exact counts of identified persons. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=16|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 16]]

The 2019–2021 EVA v7.1 table gives approximately 427 short-exposure and 3,460 long-exposure premature deaths, total about 3,890. Its rounded pollutant totals are SO2~25, O3~85, NO2 ~30 and PM2.5 ~3,740. PM2.5 includes primary particles and secondary material formed in the atmosphere. The slide lists “NH4” among emitted precursor gases; **ammonia is NH3**, while ammonium NH4+ occurs in particle salts. EEA's “Sources and emissions of air pollutants in Europe,” pollutant definitions/secondary-PM passage, verifies ammonia's precursor role: [EEA source](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/air-quality-in-europe-2022/sources-and-emissions-of-air-pollutants-in-europe). The table's rounded rows/columns need not reconcile exactly, and blank cells should not be silently interpreted as exact zero. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=17|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 17]]

On p. 18 the narrative local shares (including unexplained Copenhagen 12%, 5%, 9%) and the table are different presentations: the table explicitly concerns **2030 Nordic capital-city contributions**, giving city/country/abroad shares Copenhagen 15/23/63, Stockholm 35/18/47, Helsinki 25/21/53 and Reykjavík 43/27/30 percent. Rounding explains sums such as 101%; it does not resolve the unlabeled Copenhagen narrative figures. The common lesson is that local measures address only part of exposure, with traffic and wood stoves identified as large local sources. Retain the differing year/boundary labels instead of treating the figures as one exact estimate. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=18|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 18]]

source_units.heading: Economic standing: whose loss counts?
source_units.text:
## Economic standing: whose loss counts?

Standing chooses whose impacts enter the benefit-cost account: residents of the emitting country, EU residents, or people worldwide. Valuation then chooses Czech unit values, uniform EU values, or country-specific WTP. These are separate decisions. Physical p. 19's four perspectives—Czech narrow, Czech broad, EU and independent observer—produce different stacked cost totals and geographical shares for the same mining-limit variants. Narrow standing excludes much of the transboundary harm; broader standing includes it. The figure is therefore about ethical/policy boundaries and monetary weights as well as atmospheric science. The source article's Methods/perspectives verifies this distinction. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=19|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 19]]

The four perspectives use these distinct rules in the cited mining case:

| Perspective | Receptors whose health impacts count | Values applied to matching endpoints |
|---|---|---|
| Czech narrow | Czech population only | Czech values: EU unit values adjusted by the Czech/EU GDP per person at purchasing-power parity, about 0.82 for 2014. |
| Czech broad | All populations covered by the model, including foreign receptors | The same Czech values for every included country. |
| EU policy maker | All modelled populations; the case also includes affected non-EU receptors | Uniform EU unit values for every included country. |
| Independent observer | All modelled populations | Country-specific values, adjusting EU values by each country's relative GDP per person at purchasing-power parity. |

Thus Czech narrow versus broad changes the receptor boundary while holding the value rule fixed; Czech broad versus EU changes monetary weights with the modelled receptor boundary held fixed. The independent-observer calculation adds country-specific weights. “All modelled” is the study's finite geographical coverage, not proof that every global effect was measured. These are appraisal conventions, not claims that a person's intrinsic worth depends on GDP. The bounded manuscript's Methods/perspectives explains the rules. [Máca et al. 2017, manuscript physical pp. 3–5](https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/92550/1/MPRA_paper_92550.pdf).

The figure's **variants 1–4** are alternative territorial mining limits: 1 keeps the existing limits; 2 revokes them at Bílina only; 3 revokes them at Bílina and partly at ČSA; 4 revokes them at both mines. They alter the coal-extraction/use path over the case's 2015–2050 horizon. Within a variant, changing perspective changes whose damages and which values enter; comparing variants within one perspective changes the mining scenario. The graph should not be read as four different pollutants or four valuation rules alone. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=19|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 19]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Economic_Standing.png]]

Location-specific exposure/response and explicit standing are core because they explain why “one tonne = one universal damage price” fails. The historical plant/Danish/Nordic examples are supporting applications; their exact vintage, units and caveats remain part of their meaning. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=4|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 4–19]]

source_units.heading: Greenhouse effect, CO2 and Earth's energy
source_units.text:
# Greenhouse effect, CO2 and Earth's energy

Why does increasing atmospheric greenhouse-gas abundance alter climate, and where does the extra energy go? The lecture links radiation, concentrations and Earth's heat inventory. A temperature change is one consequence of an energy imbalance; ocean heating and ice change are also part of that response. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=20|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 20–39]]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 A[Incoming solar energy] --> B[Reflection and absorption]
 B --> C[Surface emits thermal infrared]
 D[Greenhouse gases absorb and emit infrared] --> E[Changed energy balance]
 C --> D
 F[Human emissions increase concentrations] --> D
 E --> G[Heat in ocean land atmosphere and ice]
 G --> H[Temperature and other climate effects]
 F --> I[Ocean CO2 uptake and acidification]
 H --> J[Interpret evidence using date units and baseline]
```

This source-derived map follows physical pp. 21–39 and distinguishes a radiative mechanism, its evidence and a separate chemical effect of CO2. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=21|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 21–39]]

## The radiative mechanism and its limits as an analogy

The Czech schematic on p. 22 shows incoming sunlight, some reflection by Earth's surface/atmosphere, absorption at the surface and outgoing longwave heat radiation. Greenhouse gases/clouds absorb and emit part of that infrared radiation, including downward emission. “Sluneční záření” is solar radiation, “Země” Earth and “atmosféra” atmosphere. The source's text describes this as absorption and “reflection” by greenhouse-gas molecules; the physical mechanism is absorption and re-emission, not a literal infrared mirror. The embedded comment likewise contrasts reflected sunlight and thermal radiation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=22|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 22, 24–25]]

The p. 23 historical teaching diagram gives absorbed sunlight 235 W/m², split into 67 atmospheric and 168 surface absorption. Thermal loss to space is 195+40=235 W/m²; its larger internal downward/upward flows (including 324 downward and 350 absorbed greenhouse radiation) do not create energy but redistribute it within the surface–atmosphere system. These are the figure's illustrative older-budget values, not a current measurement of every energy flux. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=23|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 23]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Greenhouse_Budget.png]]

Natural greenhouse warming makes the surface warmer than it would be without this radiative effect. **Change** in greenhouse-gas abundance enhances that natural effect and changes the balance; a natural greenhouse effect by itself is not synonymous with ongoing human-caused climate change. CO2 is a central long-lived greenhouse gas, not the only one: methane, nitrous oxide and halogenated gases also matter. The source's description of CO2 as “most important” is read in its long-lived anthropogenic context rather than ignoring water-vapour/cloud feedback. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=24|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 24–25]]

The lecture says CO2 supplied about two-thirds of the total human-produced greenhouse-gas heating influence in 2021. Keep its year and denominator; a share of total forcing and a share of the **increase since 1990** are different statistics. Its list includes “black carbon” among gases on pp. 25/48; that is a category error. Black carbon is an aerosol/soot component, not a greenhouse gas. The European Commission JRC glossary explicitly defines it as an aerosol species: [consulted definition](https://knowledge4policy.ec.europa.eu/glossary-item/black-carbon_en). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=24|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 24–25, 48]]

## Concentration is not a global daily average by default

A concentration in **ppm** measures a fraction of atmospheric molecules; Mauna Loa is a particular station, a daily/monthly average is not an annual average, and a global marine-surface estimate is not a station reading. The seasonal cycle on the Mauna Loa graphs reflects Northern Hemisphere vegetation uptake/decay over the year, superimposed on a long-term human-driven rise. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=27|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 27–29]]

The source reports global 419.3 ppm in 2023, global 422.7 ppm in 2024, and a Mauna Loa daily 425.68 ppm on 1 November 2025; the last is a source-reported dated station value, not independently reconstructed daily data. Its 2024 “increase over 2023” 3.75 ppm is not the arithmetic difference of the displayed annual means (422.7−419.3=3.4). These statements mix vintages and annual-average versus within-year growth conventions. **Reference check:** NOAA's archived 21 May 2025 article reports global 2024 annual 422.8 ppm, within-2024 increase 3.75 ppm and Mauna Loa annual 424.61 ppm. This explains why year/series/averaging definition must accompany a number; the source 422.7 differs from that reference and from its own p. 30 figure 422.8. [NOAA, “Carbon dioxide levels in 2024”](https://content-drupal.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-atmospheric-carbon-dioxide). These are documented historical comparisons, not live 2026 concentrations. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=28|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 28–30]]

Physical p. 30 compares an 800,000-year ice-core record (below about 300 ppm in that displayed record) with a modern dot. Its graphic labels **2024 average 422.8 ppm**, while the caption still says 2022. The observed lesson is the large, rapid recent rise relative to those glacial/interglacial variations; the inconsistent caption year is retained explicitly rather than relabeling the figure silently. The source attributes the underlying reconstruction to Lüthi et al. 2008/NOAA NCEI. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=30|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 30]]

## Reading the temperature evidence

Physical p. 32 is a deep-time reconstructed-temperature composite with **nonuniform time scales**: millions, then thousands of years, with geological periods and human-evolution labels. It illustrates long-run climate variation; straight visual slopes across scale changes do not measure comparable rates. Physical p. 33's heading mentions a “hockey stick dispute,” but its actual graph compares several historical temperature series over roughly 1840–2000. It is not, by itself, a millennium reconstruction or a resolution of every attribution dispute. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=32|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 32–33]]

Physical p. 34 is explicitly a **one-day average 2 m temperature field for 25 February 2018** from GFS/ClimateReanalyzer. It shows spatial weather variation, not a global multi-decade trend or an anomaly with a stated climatology. Physical p. 35 instead gives a global land/sea temperature **anomaly relative to 1961–1990**, with an 1850–2023 plotted record and grey 95% confidence bounds. An anomaly is a difference from that reference mean, not the absolute surface temperature. It cannot be directly equated with a warming target relative to a different preindustrial baseline. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=34|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 34–35]]

## Energy imbalance and the heat inventory

Incoming energy minus outgoing radiation is the net energy flux. A positive imbalance means energy accumulates in Earth's system. The source's von Schuckmann et al. 2020 figure estimates **358±37 ZJ** total heat gain over 1971–2018 (1 ZJ=$10^{21}$joules), equivalent to mean **0.47±0.10 W/m²**. Its 2010–2018 estimate is **0.87±0.12 W/m²**. These different periods must remain attached to the values. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=36|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 36–37]]

For 1971–2018, the diagram partitions heat uptake into ocean 89%, land 6%, cryosphere 4% and atmosphere 1%. Parentheses give 2010–2018 values 90%, 5%, 3%, 2%. Ocean layers account for 52% upper 0–700 m, 28% at 700–2000 m and 9% below 2000 m in the longer period, versus 52/30/8% in the later period. The ocean dominates: surface-air temperature alone does not measure all the accumulated energy. **Reference verification:** the cited original's §6 and Figure 8/caption reproduce the periods/partition and clarify the conditional calculation: [von Schuckmann et al.2020](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/12/2013/2020/). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=37|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 37]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Earth_Heat_Inventory.png]]

The figure's “−57±8 ppm” is the paper's modeled CO2 reduction from an approximately 410 ppm reference needed to counter its estimated 2010–2018 imbalance under its radiative assumptions. It is neither an observed concentration decline nor an unconditional present-day policy target. The paper also notes other greenhouse-gas changes affect that calculation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=37|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 37]]

Physical p. 38 shows ocean-heat-content anomalies relative to 2005–2017 for 0–300, 0–700, 0–2000 and 700–2000 m layers, with ensemble 2σ shading. Some depth bands overlap, so adding all curves would double count heat. The caption specifies the ocean area 60°S–60°N and bathymetry restrictions for the contributing products; do not generalize its per-area axis into an unqualified global total. Rising curves and uncertainty bands support ocean warming within that study coverage. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=38|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 38]]

## CO2 also changes ocean chemistry

CO2 dissolving into seawater changes carbonate chemistry and lowers pH. Physical p. 39 reports surface-ocean pH falling from 8.21 to 8.10 since industrialization and contrasts an intact shell with one exposed to more corrosive conditions. “Acidification” means decreasing pH; it does not mean the average seawater has already become acidic in the everyday pH<7 sense. The shell comparison illustrates a biological consequence but supplies no full experiment protocol for estimating an effect size. This chemical pathway is distinct from the radiative-heating pathway even though both start with increased CO2. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=39|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 39]]

The core foundations are radiation/energy conservation, concentration-versus-emission units and period/reference baselines, because those distinctions keep every graph interpretable. Historical temperatures and the shell image support these mechanisms without becoming current datasets or independent causal estimates. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=22|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 22–39]]

source_units.text:
## The radiative mechanism and its limits as an analogy

The Czech schematic on p. 22 shows incoming sunlight, some reflection by Earth's surface/atmosphere, absorption at the surface and outgoing longwave heat radiation. Greenhouse gases/clouds absorb and emit part of that infrared radiation, including downward emission. “Sluneční záření” is solar radiation, “Země” Earth and “atmosféra” atmosphere. The source's text describes this as absorption and “reflection” by greenhouse-gas molecules; the physical mechanism is absorption and re-emission, not a literal infrared mirror. The embedded comment likewise contrasts reflected sunlight and thermal radiation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=22|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 22, 24–25]]

The p. 23 historical teaching diagram gives absorbed sunlight 235 W/m², split into 67 atmospheric and 168 surface absorption. Thermal loss to space is 195+40=235 W/m²; its larger internal downward/upward flows (including 324 downward and 350 absorbed greenhouse radiation) do not create energy but redistribute it within the surface–atmosphere system. These are the figure's illustrative older-budget values, not a current measurement of every energy flux. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=23|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 23]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Greenhouse_Budget.png]]

Natural greenhouse warming makes the surface warmer than it would be without this radiative effect. **Change** in greenhouse-gas abundance enhances that natural effect and changes the balance; a natural greenhouse effect by itself is not synonymous with ongoing human-caused climate change. CO2 is a central long-lived greenhouse gas, not the only one: methane, nitrous oxide and halogenated gases also matter. The source's description of CO2 as “most important” is read in its long-lived anthropogenic context rather than ignoring water-vapour/cloud feedback. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=24|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 24–25]]

The lecture says CO2 supplied about two-thirds of the total human-produced greenhouse-gas heating influence in 2021. Keep its year and denominator; a share of total forcing and a share of the **increase since 1990** are different statistics. Its list includes “black carbon” among gases on pp. 25/48; that is a category error. Black carbon is an aerosol/soot component, not a greenhouse gas. The European Commission JRC glossary explicitly defines it as an aerosol species: [consulted definition](https://knowledge4policy.ec.europa.eu/glossary-item/black-carbon_en). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=24|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 24–25, 48]]

source_units.heading: Energy imbalance and the heat inventory
source_units.text:
## Energy imbalance and the heat inventory

Incoming energy minus outgoing radiation is the net energy flux. A positive imbalance means energy accumulates in Earth's system. The source's von Schuckmann et al. 2020 figure estimates **358±37 ZJ** total heat gain over 1971–2018 (1 ZJ=$10^{21}$joules), equivalent to mean **0.47±0.10 W/m²**. Its 2010–2018 estimate is **0.87±0.12 W/m²**. These different periods must remain attached to the values. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=36|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 36–37]]

For 1971–2018, the diagram partitions heat uptake into ocean 89%, land 6%, cryosphere 4% and atmosphere 1%. Parentheses give 2010–2018 values 90%, 5%, 3%, 2%. Ocean layers account for 52% upper 0–700 m, 28% at 700–2000 m and 9% below 2000 m in the longer period, versus 52/30/8% in the later period. The ocean dominates: surface-air temperature alone does not measure all the accumulated energy. **Reference verification:** the cited original's §6 and Figure 8/caption reproduce the periods/partition and clarify the conditional calculation: [von Schuckmann et al.2020](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/12/2013/2020/). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=37|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 37]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Earth_Heat_Inventory.png]]

The figure's “−57±8 ppm” is the paper's modeled CO2 reduction from an approximately 410 ppm reference needed to counter its estimated 2010–2018 imbalance under its radiative assumptions. It is neither an observed concentration decline nor an unconditional present-day policy target. The paper also notes other greenhouse-gas changes affect that calculation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=37|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 37]]

Physical p. 38 shows ocean-heat-content anomalies relative to 2005–2017 for 0–300, 0–700, 0–2000 and 700–2000 m layers, with ensemble 2σ shading. Some depth bands overlap, so adding all curves would double count heat. The caption specifies the ocean area 60°S–60°N and bathymetry restrictions for the contributing products; do not generalize its per-area axis into an unqualified global total. Rising curves and uncertainty bands support ocean warming within that study coverage. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=38|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 38]]

source_units.heading: CO2 also changes ocean chemistry
source_units.text:
## CO2 also changes ocean chemistry

CO2 dissolving into seawater changes carbonate chemistry and lowers pH. Physical p. 39 reports surface-ocean pH falling from 8.21 to 8.10 since industrialization and contrasts an intact shell with one exposed to more corrosive conditions. “Acidification” means decreasing pH; it does not mean the average seawater has already become acidic in the everyday pH<7 sense. The shell comparison illustrates a biological consequence but supplies no full experiment protocol for estimating an effect size. This chemical pathway is distinct from the radiative-heating pathway even though both start with increased CO2. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=39|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 39]]

The core foundations are radiation/energy conservation, concentration-versus-emission units and period/reference baselines, because those distinctions keep every graph interpretable. Historical temperatures and the shell image support these mechanisms without becoming current datasets or independent causal estimates. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=22|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 22–39]]

source_units.heading: Concentration is not a global daily average by default
source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/Greenhouse_Effect_CO2_and_Earth_Energy.md#Concentration is not a global daily average by default
source_units.text:
## Concentration is not a global daily average by default

A concentration in **ppm** measures a fraction of atmospheric molecules; Mauna Loa is a particular station, a daily/monthly average is not an annual average, and a global marine-surface estimate is not a station reading. The seasonal cycle on the Mauna Loa graphs reflects Northern Hemisphere vegetation uptake/decay over the year, superimposed on a long-term human-driven rise. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=27|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 27–29]]

The source reports global 419.3 ppm in 2023, global 422.7 ppm in 2024, and a Mauna Loa daily 425.68 ppm on 1 November 2025; the last is a source-reported dated station value, not independently reconstructed daily data. Its 2024 “increase over 2023” 3.75 ppm is not the arithmetic difference of the displayed annual means (422.7−419.3=3.4). These statements mix vintages and annual-average versus within-year growth conventions. **Reference check:** NOAA's archived 21 May 2025 article reports global 2024 annual 422.8 ppm, within-2024 increase 3.75 ppm and Mauna Loa annual 424.61 ppm. This explains why year/series/averaging definition must accompany a number; the source 422.7 differs from that reference and from its own p. 30 figure 422.8. [NOAA, “Carbon dioxide levels in 2024”](https://content-drupal.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-atmospheric-carbon-dioxide). These are documented historical comparisons, not live 2026 concentrations. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=28|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 28–30]]

Physical p. 30 compares an 800,000-year ice-core record (below about 300 ppm in that displayed record) with a modern dot. Its graphic labels **2024 average 422.8 ppm**, while the caption still says 2022. The observed lesson is the large, rapid recent rise relative to those glacial/interglacial variations; the inconsistent caption year is retained explicitly rather than relabeling the figure silently. The source attributes the underlying reconstruction to Lüthi et al. 2008/NOAA NCEI. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=30|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 30]]

source_units.heading: Reading the temperature evidence
source_units.text:
## Reading the temperature evidence

Physical p. 32 is a deep-time reconstructed-temperature composite with **nonuniform time scales**: millions, then thousands of years, with geological periods and human-evolution labels. It illustrates long-run climate variation; straight visual slopes across scale changes do not measure comparable rates. Physical p. 33's heading mentions a “hockey stick dispute,” but its actual graph compares several historical temperature series over roughly 1840–2000. It is not, by itself, a millennium reconstruction or a resolution of every attribution dispute. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=32|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 32–33]]

Physical p. 34 is explicitly a **one-day average 2 m temperature field for 25 February 2018** from GFS/ClimateReanalyzer. It shows spatial weather variation, not a global multi-decade trend or an anomaly with a stated climatology. Physical p. 35 instead gives a global land/sea temperature **anomaly relative to 1961–1990**, with an 1850–2023 plotted record and grey 95% confidence bounds. An anomaly is a difference from that reference mean, not the absolute surface temperature. It cannot be directly equated with a warming target relative to a different preindustrial baseline. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=34|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 34–35]]

source_units.heading: Carbon units, stocks, flows and emissions charts
source_units.key: 01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/Carbon_Units_Stocks_Flows_and_Emissions_Charts.md#Carbon units, stocks, flows and emissions charts
source_units.text:
# Carbon units, stocks, flows and emissions charts

Which quantities can be compared when a chart says carbon, CO2, CO2-equivalent, concentration or per person? The optional-reading section supplies unit conversions and charts. Reading their units and boundaries is a foundation for both climate-policy comparisons and monetary costs per tonne. These pages are included because they are inside the selected supplied document, while retaining their “Voluntary readings” status. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=46|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 46–58]]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 A[What quantity is measured] --> B[Carbon mass versus CO2 mass]
 A --> C[CO2 equivalent with stated metric horizon]
 A --> D[Concentration stock versus emission flow]
 B --> E[Consistent prices per tonne]
 C --> F[Compare gas and sector emissions]
 D --> G[Stable positive emissions can increase stock]
 F --> H[Total versus per person and population]
 H --> I[Check year source boundary and causality]
```

The map follows pp. 47–58 and uses p. 26's GWP definition to separate mass conversion from warming equivalence. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=26|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 26, 47–58]]

## Carbon mass and the inverse price conversion

A tonne of carbon (t C) measures carbon atoms; a tonne of CO2 measures the whole molecule. Using source atomic masses 12 for C and 16 for O, molecular mass is $12+2(16)=44$. Therefore

$$1\ \mathrm{tCO_2}=\frac{12}{44}\ \mathrm{tC}\approx0.2727\ \mathrm{tC},\qquad
1\ \mathrm{tC}=\frac{44}{12}\ \mathrm{tCO_2}\approx3.667\ \mathrm{tCO_2}.$$

For the **same total payment**, multiplying mass by $44/12$ requires dividing price per mass by $44/12$. Thus

$$100\ \$/\mathrm{tC}\times\frac{12}{44}=27.27\ \$/\mathrm{tCO_2},\qquad
100\ \$/\mathrm{tCO_2}\times\frac{44}{12}=366.67\ \$/\mathrm{tC}.$$

Confusing quantity conversion with price conversion reverses the comparison. Neither operation is a GWP conversion for methane or other gases. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=48|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 48]]

## GWP and CO2-equivalent emissions

Global warming potential (GWP) compares the time-integrated radiative effect of a pulse mass of gas with an equal mass of CO2 over a stated horizon; CO2's value is one by definition. For a chosen metric, horizon and assessment,

$$E_{CO_2e}=\sum_g m_g GWP_g,$$

where $m_g$ is emitted mass of gas $g$. This is **agent-expanded notation** for the source's examples, not a new emissions estimate. A million tonnes of CH4 at GWP100=25 becomes 25 million tonnes CO2e; a million tonnes of N2O at 298 becomes 298 million tonnes CO2e. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=25|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 25–26, 53]]

The p. 26 table explicitly identifies **IPCC AR4 (2007)** values; retain that vintage. Its complete entries are:

| Gas | Lifetime, years | GWP20 | GWP100 | GWP500 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CH4 | 12 | 72 | 25 | 7.6 |
| N2O | 114 | 289 | 298 | 153 |
| HFC-23 | 270 | 12000 | 14800 | 12200 |
| HFC-134a | 14 | 3830 | 1430 | 425 |
| SF6 | 3200 | 16300 | 22800 | 32600 |

These are the supplied historical values, not current universal constants or evidence that later charts use exactly the same assessment. A CO2e label needs its horizon and metric convention for exact comparison. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=26|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 26]]

## Trace-gas concentration and AGGI

Physical p. 47 uses ppm for CO2, ppb for CH4/N2O and ppt for halocarbons. Each panel has its own scale. The historical plots show rising CO2, CH4 and N2O, peaking/declining CFC-11/CFC-12, and rising HCFC-22/HFC-134a over their displayed period ending around 2020. Heights across separate axes are not direct abundance comparisons. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=47|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 47]]

Physical p. 49 contrasts CO2-alone concentration with a **CO2-equivalent mixing ratio** obtained by matching forcing from long-lived gases, and a separate AGGI right axis. This equivalent concentration is not a sum of GWP-weighted emission tonnes. The slide does not explain AGGI's baseline. **Supplementary definition:** NOAA defines AGGI as long-lived-gas effective radiative forcing relative to its 1990 value, making 1990 equal one. It is a forcing ratio, not an emissions flow or forecast. [NOAA AGGI, Introduction](https://gml.noaa.gov/aggi/aggi.html). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=49|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 49]]

## Why a stable flow can increase an atmospheric stock

Concentration measures an atmospheric stock; emissions add mass per unit time and sinks remove it. A simple **agent synthesis** of this accounting is

$$A_{t+1}-A_t=E_t-R_t,$$

where $A_t$ is atmospheric mass, $E_t$ emissions and $R_t$ net removal over the same interval, all in compatible mass units. A constant positive emission flow still increases $A$ whenever $E_t>R_t$. Stabilizing emissions differs from bringing **net additions** to zero. Connecting mass to ppm requires an atmospheric-mass conversion, which the source does not supply. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=50|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 50–51]]

Physical p. 50 uses separate axes for concentration (ppm) and annual emissions (gigatonnes). Its 1751–2022 graph and caption's historical increase from about 5 Gt/year in the mid twentieth century to over 35 Gt/year illustrate different quantities, not a fitted causal coefficient. Physical p. 51 draws a flat emission line and rising concentration curve on uncalibrated x1–x20 axes with no dates, units or source. Its curved stock path does not follow from constant **net** additions alone, which would give a linear stock rise. Use it for stock-flow intuition, not a quantitative carbon-cycle law. NOAA's atmospheric-CO2 article independently explains that emissions exceeding sinks raise atmospheric abundance: [“Fossil fuels overwhelm Earth's natural carbon cycle”](https://content-drupal.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-atmospheric-carbon-dioxide). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=50|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 50–51]]

## Sector quantities: gas and denominator first

Physical p. 52 is **2020 world per-capita CO2**, with these displayed sector values in tonnes per person for the reported year: electricity/heat 1.93, transport 0.91, manufacturing/construction 0.79, buildings 0.35, industry 0.21, land-use/forestry 0.15, aviation/shipping 0.12 and fugitive emissions 0.03. It credits Climate Watch (2023) and population sources (2023). It is not an all-gas CO2e total, and no finer time aggregation is supplied. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=52|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 52]]

Physical p. 53 instead shows CH4 and N2O in **CO2e**, roughly 1990–2021, with a GWP100 footnote. Agriculture is largest in each panel; methane also has substantial fugitive and waste emissions. The other methane series are land-use/forestry, other fuel combustion and industry; the other N2O series are industry, waste, land-use/forestry, fugitive and other fuel combustion. The panels have different scales, so their line heights do not directly compare gas mass. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=53|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 53]]

Physical p. 54 combines all-gas CO2e by sector: electricity/heat, transport, manufacturing/construction, agriculture, fugitive emissions, industry, buildings, waste, land-use/forestry, aviation/shipping and other fuel combustion. Its source is Climate Watch (2023). End-period downturns in some historical series do not establish a permanent future trend. Exact comparison with the AR4 table requires checking the chart dataset's assessment convention, which the slide does not establish. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=54|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 54]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Emissions_By_Sector.png]]

The complete graphic preserves each sector and its 100-year CO2e qualification. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=54|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 54]]

## Per person, population and totals

Physical p. 55 encodes per-person emissions by rectangle **height**, population by **width**, and total emissions by **area**. A populous country can have a large area but lower per-person emissions than a small country. Labels emphasize countries with large totals rather than a complete per-capita ranking. Its title says CO2 but the vertical axis says tCO2e, so the supplied graphic leaves the gas/metric boundary ambiguous; do not silently treat the two labels as interchangeable. The illustration lacks a clear data-year citation and is not a current league table. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=55|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 55]]

The p. 56 map reports 2020 total GHG CO2e per person including land-use/forestry, credits Climate Watch (2023), and has a negative legend range and hatched “no data.” The p. 57 map reports 2021 CO2/CH4/N2O in GWP100 CO2e including land-use, credits Jones et al. (2023), and notes that land-use emissions can be negative. Different years, sources and gas/boundary labels mean their visual differences cannot be read as one harmonized annual change. Negative net land-use emissions and missing data are different categories: hatching is not zero emissions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=56|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 56–57]]

Physical p. 58 compares 2018 CO2 per person with GDP per person in 2011 international dollars adjusted for purchasing power and inflation. Its GDP axis is **logarithmic** ($1000, $2000, $5000, $10000, $20000, $50000), so equal plot distances are not equal dollar increments. Emissions cover **fossil fuels and cement**, explicitly excluding land-use change. The positive cross-country association has considerable variation and does not identify a causal effect of income. Sources are the Global Carbon Project and Maddison Project Database 2020 (Bolt and van Zanden, 2020). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=58|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 58]]

Unit consistency, stock-flow accounting and total-versus-per-person denominators are core foundations because they unlock these comparisons. Historical charts remain context; none is relabeled as current or used as an unqualified causal estimate. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=47|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 47–58]]

## Why a stable flow can increase an atmospheric stock

Concentration measures an atmospheric stock; emissions add mass per unit time and sinks remove it. A simple **agent synthesis** of this accounting is

$$A_{t+1}-A_t=E_t-R_t,$$

where $A_t$ is atmospheric mass, $E_t$ emissions and $R_t$ net removal over the same interval, all in compatible mass units. A constant positive emission flow still increases $A$ whenever $E_t>R_t$. Stabilizing emissions differs from bringing **net additions** to zero. Connecting mass to ppm requires an atmospheric-mass conversion, which the source does not supply. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=50|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 50–51]]

Physical p. 50 uses separate axes for concentration (ppm) and annual emissions (gigatonnes). Its 1751–2022 graph and caption's historical increase from about 5 Gt/year in the mid twentieth century to over 35 Gt/year illustrate different quantities, not a fitted causal coefficient. Physical p. 51 draws a flat emission line and rising concentration curve on uncalibrated x1–x20 axes with no dates, units or source. Its curved stock path does not follow from constant **net** additions alone, which would give a linear stock rise. Use it for stock-flow intuition, not a quantitative carbon-cycle law. NOAA's atmospheric-CO2 article independently explains that emissions exceeding sinks raise atmospheric abundance: [“Fossil fuels overwhelm Earth's natural carbon cycle”](https://content-drupal.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-atmospheric-carbon-dioxide). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=50|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 50–51]]

source_units.heading: Sector quantities: gas and denominator first
source_units.text:
## Sector quantities: gas and denominator first

Physical p. 52 is **2020 world per-capita CO2**, with these displayed sector values in tonnes per person for the reported year: electricity/heat 1.93, transport 0.91, manufacturing/construction 0.79, buildings 0.35, industry 0.21, land-use/forestry 0.15, aviation/shipping 0.12 and fugitive emissions 0.03. It credits Climate Watch (2023) and population sources (2023). It is not an all-gas CO2e total, and no finer time aggregation is supplied. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=52|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 52]]

Physical p. 53 instead shows CH4 and N2O in **CO2e**, roughly 1990–2021, with a GWP100 footnote. Agriculture is largest in each panel; methane also has substantial fugitive and waste emissions. The other methane series are land-use/forestry, other fuel combustion and industry; the other N2O series are industry, waste, land-use/forestry, fugitive and other fuel combustion. The panels have different scales, so their line heights do not directly compare gas mass. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=53|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 53]]

Physical p. 54 combines all-gas CO2e by sector: electricity/heat, transport, manufacturing/construction, agriculture, fugitive emissions, industry, buildings, waste, land-use/forestry, aviation/shipping and other fuel combustion. Its source is Climate Watch (2023). End-period downturns in some historical series do not establish a permanent future trend. Exact comparison with the AR4 table requires checking the chart dataset's assessment convention, which the slide does not establish. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=54|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 54]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Emissions_By_Sector.png]]

The complete graphic preserves each sector and its 100-year CO2e qualification. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=54|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 54]]

source_units.heading: Per person, population and totals
source_units.text:
## Per person, population and totals

Physical p. 55 encodes per-person emissions by rectangle **height**, population by **width**, and total emissions by **area**. A populous country can have a large area but lower per-person emissions than a small country. Labels emphasize countries with large totals rather than a complete per-capita ranking. Its title says CO2 but the vertical axis says tCO2e, so the supplied graphic leaves the gas/metric boundary ambiguous; do not silently treat the two labels as interchangeable. The illustration lacks a clear data-year citation and is not a current league table. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=55|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 55]]

The p. 56 map reports 2020 total GHG CO2e per person including land-use/forestry, credits Climate Watch (2023), and has a negative legend range and hatched “no data.” The p. 57 map reports 2021 CO2/CH4/N2O in GWP100 CO2e including land-use, credits Jones et al. (2023), and notes that land-use emissions can be negative. Different years, sources and gas/boundary labels mean their visual differences cannot be read as one harmonized annual change. Negative net land-use emissions and missing data are different categories: hatching is not zero emissions. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=56|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 56–57]]

Physical p. 58 compares 2018 CO2 per person with GDP per person in 2011 international dollars adjusted for purchasing power and inflation. Its GDP axis is **logarithmic** ($1000, $2000, $5000, $10000, $20000, $50000), so equal plot distances are not equal dollar increments. Emissions cover **fossil fuels and cement**, explicitly excluding land-use change. The positive cross-country association has considerable variation and does not identify a causal effect of income. Sources are the Global Carbon Project and Maddison Project Database 2020 (Bolt and van Zanden, 2020). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=58|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 58]]

Unit consistency, stock-flow accounting and total-versus-per-person denominators are core foundations because they unlock these comparisons. Historical charts remain context; none is relabeled as current or used as an unqualified causal estimate. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=47|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 47–58]]

source_units.heading: Climate scenarios, policy and adaptation
source_units.text:
# Climate scenarios, policy and adaptation

A climate scenario asks what follows **if** a coherent set of social, technological, emissions and policy conditions occurs. It is not an assigned probability or an unconditional forecast. The lecture uses older RCP projections alongside newer SSP-labelled examples; the two naming systems and their temperature baselines must be distinguished. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=40|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 40–45]]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 A[Socioeconomic assumptions] --> B[Emissions pathway]
 C[Policy choices] --> B
 B --> D[Concentrations and radiative forcing]
 D --> E[Conditional climate projection]
 E --> F[Impacts and risks]
 C --> G[Mitigation reduces drivers]
 F --> H[Adaptation manages remaining impacts]
 I[Scenario label period baseline uncertainty] --> E
```

This map follows pp. 40–45 and 43's paired emissions/concentration graphic; it explains why the policy discussion needs both mitigation and adaptation. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=40|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 40–45]]

## SSP assumptions and RCP forcing pathways

The source presents **SSP2**, “middle of the road,” as its baseline socioeconomic narrative, extending major development trends without a large assumed policy/technology break. That is the lecture's baseline choice, not a universal definition that SSP2 equals one forcing outcome. Shared Socioeconomic Pathways describe demographic, economic and technological narratives; Representative Concentration Pathways describe emissions/concentration/forcing trajectories. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=41|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 41, 43]]

Radiative forcing measures a change in Earth's energy balance in **W/m²**, as the embedded comments on pp. 41–42 explain. RCP labels 2.6/4.5/6.0/8.5 refer to approximate 2100 forcing levels, with different trajectories toward them. The source associates 2.6/4.5/6.0 with approximately 490/650/850 ppm CO2-equivalent and leaves 8.5 unfinished. These are the slide's older shorthand values, not concentrations of CO2 alone; the exact trajectory and whether a quoted value is a peak or endpoint matter. Its claim that forcing is “declining” should not be read as monotonic decline throughout every RCP. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=41|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 41]]

There is a source inconsistency: p. 41 calls RCP6.0 “close to SSP2,” whereas p. 42 calls RCP8.5 “close to SSP2.” A socioeconomic family does not uniquely identify a forcing path. **Authoritative clarification:** IPCC AR6 WGI SPM BoxSPM.1 and note 22 define **SSPx-y** as socioeconomic family x plus approximate 2100 forcing y. The supplied p. 43 itself shows SSP2-4.5 as intermediate, alongside SSP1-1.9/SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0/SSP5-8.5. [IPCC AR6 WGI SPM, BoxSPM.1/note22](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/summary-for-policymakers/). Thus neither conflicting “close to” statement is used as a one-to-one mapping. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=41|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 41–43]]

## The AR5 temperature table needs its reference period

The supplied p. 42 table reports the following **°C changes relative to 1986–2005**, verified from IPCC 2014 Synthesis Report Table 2.1 (printed p. 60 and its notes). That missing baseline is essential: these are not automatically additional temperatures above the Paris preindustrial reference. Entries are means with the source's likely ranges; scenarios are conditional, and range width is not a probability assigned to the scenario itself. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=42|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 42]]

| RCP |2046–2065 mean (likely range),°C|2081–2100 mean (likely range),°C|
|---|---|---|
|2.6|1.0 (0.4–1.6)|1.0 (0.3–1.7)|
|4.5|1.4 (0.9–2.0)|1.8 (1.1–2.6)|
|6.0|1.3 (0.8–1.8)|2.2 (1.4–3.1)|
|8.5|2.0 (1.4–2.6)|3.7 (2.6–4.8)|

The official table notes natural variability, forcing/model uncertainty and different confidence for the two horizons. Its observed baseline offset is not itself a complete uncertainty conversion rule, so do not add a constant and reuse the identical uncertainty range without qualification. [IPCC2014 Synthesis Report, Table2.1 and notes](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full.pdf). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=42|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 42]]

![[01_Notes/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/assets/Week_3_Emissions_Concentration_Scenarios.png]]

Physical p. 43 compares annual CO2 emissions (billions of tonnes/year) with resulting atmospheric CO2 concentrations (ppm). Low-emission paths bend down and can become net negative; concentrations need not follow emissions one-for-one because they reflect accumulated additions and removals. The caption says only central illustrative curves are shown, not the full uncertainty distribution. This graphic therefore illustrates scenario mechanisms rather than exact forecasts. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=43|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 43]]

## Climate policy: source claims and verified chronology

Physical p. 44 names the UNFCCC, Kyoto arrangements and annual Conferences of the Parties (COPs). It refers to Annex I/II groupings and writes “DCM, JI”; the recognized Kyoto project mechanism is **CDM, Clean Development Mechanism**, alongside Joint Implementation. Annex groupings/targets are not all interchangeable: the official Kyoto overview distinguishes the Convention's annex structure and Kyoto Annex B commitments. Only that overview is needed here, not an invented treaty-law curriculum. **Correction:** the slide's “1996 Kyoto Protocol” is wrong; Kyoto was adopted 11 December 1997 and entered into force 16 February 2005. [UNFCCC Kyoto overview, opening/market mechanisms](https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-kyoto-protocol). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=44|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 44]]

The lecture describes Paris COP21 in 2015 as pursuing warming well below 2°C and efforts toward 1.5°C above preindustrial levels, with peaking as soon as possible and rapid subsequent reductions. Its discussion of INDCs concerns the pledges at that historical conference, not a checked present-day assessment of every NDC. The slide calls 4 November 2016 a “ratification” date; it is the Agreement's **entry into force** date. Adoption was 12 December 2015; individual parties ratify on their own dates. [UNFCCC Paris overview](https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-paris-agreement). [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=44|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 44]]

The slide's subsequent conference list runs through COP30/Brazil 2025, naming Marrakesh 2016, Bonn 2017, Katowice 2018, Madrid 2019, the 2020 pandemic gap, Glasgow 2021, Cairo 2022, Dubai 2023 and Baku 2024. **Location correction:** COP27 was in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, not Cairo; the official proceedings state its 2022 venue. [UNFCCC COP27 proceedings listing](https://unfccc.int/event/cop-27). These are the source's historical orientation, not a live future meeting schedule. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=44|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 44]]

## Mitigation and adaptation solve different parts of the problem

Mitigation reduces climate-change drivers, such as net greenhouse-gas emissions; adaptation changes exposure/vulnerability and responses to climatic effects that still occur. Physical p. 45 combines a historical/projected warming panel with five escalating risk categories—unique/threatened systems, extreme weather, distribution of impacts, global aggregate impacts and large-scale singular events. Coloured transitions represent increasing risk, not cash damages or a uniform threshold for all outcomes. It overlays Paris NDC/aspiration labels on an AR5-era figure and concludes that even successful mitigation leaves impacts requiring adaptation. Read the overlay as a teaching illustration, not a current quantified forecast of the Paris pledges. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=45|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 45]]

The core reading path is assumptions→emissions→forcing→conditional climate→risks, then the complementary responses. Matching scenario type, baseline, date and uncertainty is prerequisite to using the numbers; conference chronology is supporting context with the source errors explicitly repaired here. [[00_Materials/2026_2027/Winter_Semester/Economics_of_Green_Deal/Week_3/02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf#page=40|02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 40–45]]
